1.	A discussion as to the establishment oi a fair wages board or boards has taken place with the representatives of the labour organizations. The discussion also had reference to the application of the Industrial Disputes Act in such cases.
2.	The subject has been discussed with the chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board.

A fair wages clause is inserted by the Government of Canada for all contracts for supplies and munitions of war which are ordered by the Canadian Government for the Canadian Military forces. There is therefore no reason whatever from the standpoint of the Canadian Government why the contracts placed by the British Government in Canada should not contain a fair wages clause. In adopting that course the British Government would be directly in line with the course which has been pursued by the Canadian Government in its own contracts. The representatives of the Labour Organizations have been informed that the Government of Canada has no control whatever over the form or nature of such contracts, but that their suggestions would be recommended to the consideration of the British Government.

As an evidence of our continued activity in the United States, and of our desire to act in co-operation with the 'western, provinces, the following letter from the Premier of Saskatchewan is presented:
Regina, 17th February, 1916. Dear Sir Robert:
Mr. Calder has shown me your letter to him of 22nd January acknowledging receipt of the joint resolution of the prairie province governments upon immigration work in the United States. All that you say and the suggestions and requests which you offer in relation to the co-ordination of Dominion and Provincial activities are very satisfactory indeed. In the meantime I attended, on Dr. Roche's invitation, the conference of federal agents held at Chicago, January 28, talcing downl with me Mr. Auld, our Acting Deputy Minister of Agriculture. I was highly satisfied with the spirit and proceedings of the Conference. From it I came away convinced that any impression existing that the United States agents had been relaxing their efforts was an entirely mistaken impression. For the recent disappointing results the agents are not to blame; they have continued working zealously in face of extremely discouraging conditions. In some respects their hands may be considerably strengthened by arrangements which will ensure to them more specific, regular and prompt information of affairs in Western Canada, and in this matter Mr. Auld's Department can assist and will assist in future in every possible way. You are of course aware that the Saskatchewan Government maintains that as long as your Government controls our public lands and other natural resources the implied guaranty given in 1905 should be respected, viz; that your Government should be responsible for all outlays for colonization in behalf of Saskatchewan. We have never entered upon immigration work, and will not do so until the control of public resources is transferred to us, but to the extent to which any machinery we have in existence can be used in helping your Government's efforts, we are earnestly desirous of assisting.
Believe me,
Very sincerely yours,

speakeroldname: Mr. S. FRANK GLASS (East Middlesex) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, taking into consideration the stability of the flax industry and the market value of the product, more attention might be given to promoting its cultivation in Canada ; that the flax and linen industries should, both as to culture and manufacture, receive that aid and cor s 'deration from the Government, which would enable it to assume the importance the natural resources of our country assure it. And to this end, serious encouragement should be given to farmers by such means as the Government, after full investigation, deem best to increase the production of flax throughout the Dominion.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I desire at the
outset to say that I have been prompted to introduce this resolution as a result of observations in the districts surrounding that from which I come, and of representations made to me and to other hon. members, all tending to show that, owing to the very unusual conditions which prevail at the present time by reason of the destruction of the flax industry in the countries of Europe who are at war, it is peculiarly desirable that the Government of Canada should take advantage of the opportunity now presented to put the flax industry of this country on a stable foundation. When I placed the notice of motion on the Order Paper I was not aware that my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) had already taken the matter up. I desire just here to say that my hon. friend

from East Lambton has, during the recess, been very active in promoting the interests of the flax-growers in that part of western Ontario where the production of flax for fibre has reached its highest development. Before proceeding with the discussion of this subject 1 would like to present to the House, and record in Hansard, the views of flax-growers of western Ontario, who have, on their own initiative and in their own interest, stimulated as they have been by the unusual conditions, taken steps to promote the development of this industry. I believe that Mr Howard Fraleigh, ,of the village of Forest, Lambton county, is generally looked upon as one of the most capable and best informed men on this subject to be found within the confines of our country. He has been a successful man and he has given a great deal of time to research, study, and experiment in connection with all branches of the question of fibre production from flax. He is president of the association in the province of Ontario; and, in giving his ideas as to how the Government may best co-operate in promoting an increased production of flax, he suggests the following:
1.	Closer co-operation between the departments of the Government and flax men. For example, the experimental stations can scarcely do the flax growers much good unless they investigate wherein we need assistance. Again, it does not by any means follow that, because poor samples of flax may be grown on the Experimental Farm at Ottawa, the whole Dominion is unsuitable for the crop. Some such propaganda as the teaching of farmers what are the peculiar needs of flax in the way of cultivation would be advisable.
2.	The establishment of a flax bureau or commission, composed of men who understand flax and have its interests at heart. This bureau to have charge of the activities looking to improved methods of cultivation and manufacture, the education of the public in the true facts about flax, and the introduction of standards of grading both seed and fibre for export.
3.	Encouragement by the Department of Commerce in building up a greater linen industry at home.
4.	Some sort of bonus to growers of flax for fibre purposes, same to take effect after the war prices decline, and remain in force until the industry becomes re-established again.
5.	Government assistance to manufacturers in securing flax workers by encouraging immigration of Irish and Belgian flax-workers; or courses of instruction to young Canadians, such as are carried on in Ireland. Such courses could be given at the big agricultural colleges.
6.	Government encouragement to farmers to grow more flax, not only for their own profit, but to help nearby towns, and the Dominion at large.
7.	A series of government experiments, in collaboration with the growers, to determine whether water-retting can be successfully carried on in Canada on a commercial scale.

S.	Immediate and temporary assistance to our organization, as by the payment of the salary of our secretary, who is devoting his time to this work. Such assistance is extended to other organizations of an agricultural nature.

In connection with this subject, I have naturally found it necessary to make some investigations and to study the question from different standpoints, and I am indebted for a good' deal of the information I have been able to procure to the records of the Department of Agriculture of our own country as well as to the United States and to various states of the Union. In view of the very great importance of the subject at this particular time, I have prepared the observations which I have to make, and I would ask the indulgence of the House while I give them such information as I have been able to procure, hoping that it will impress upon the members of the House the need of this industry for assistance.
'Considering the various difficulties that flax culture has undergone in this country through the experience of many years, it may well be considered one of the curiosities of agriculture. There is nothing strange or unusual in the methods of cultivating flax as compared with cereals generally; nevertheless, there are features connected with its history that make the flax crop unique among agricultural products. The cultivation of flax and the manufacture of its fibre, date back to a very remote period. The great value of the plant has been known and appreciated for some thousands of years. The fact that Egyptian mummies were wrapped in linen proves that the use of flax fibre is very ancient. It is said that it was a well established [DOT] industry in Egypt at the dawn of the Christian era. Some three thousand years ago the Phoenicians devoted much attention to the cultivation of the plant, and subsequently the 'Greeks and Romans made the working of flax fibre a part of the household duties.
The flax plant is the source of two extremely valuable economic products, the one a fibre derived from the straw and noted from time immemorial the world over for its strength, beauty, fineness, and length of staple; the other, a seed rich in oil of such superior drying qualities as render it an indispensable ingredient in paint and varnish, and in the manufacture of linoleum, oilcloth, printer's ink, patent leather and other products. The full value, however, of both seed and straw from the one crop does not seem to have been realized

on a large scale in practical agriculture. The fibre, next to cotton, is the most valuable and universally employed textile in the whole range of vegetable fibres, and the plant can be grown in almost every part of the world where the climate is temperate. It has been cultivated to a considerable extent in Great Britain, Ireland, Sweden, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, France, Kussia, Germany, Austria, Spain, and Portugal, and likewise in many portions of North and South America. Eecent investigations and statistics show that-of the world's total production in the year 1911, South America produced 33 per cent, Eussia 22 per cent, India 18 per cent, United States 18 per cent, Canada 5 per cent, and other countries 4 per cent. So that, if the ratio of production for the last year prior to the war, or even say for the year 1914, were the same as in 1910, it is evident, in view of the fact that the countries engaged in the world-wide war were producers of 49 per cent of the world's crop in 1914, that there must necessarily have been an enormous shrinkage of the world's supply of flax during the year 1915, and that this shrinkage will be likely much greater during the coming year and for some years to come.
It would seem that the time for active effort to increase production in Canada has arrived. In the year 1908 the Government of this country, through the Department of Agriculture, made some investigations relating to the industry in Canada, which resulted in the publication of a pamphlet by the department, giving some useful information. But it appears that this was not in any way followed up, or the research or experiments continued with a view of giving any permanent assistance to the industry, and as a result valuable time has been lost. It is a matter that may be questioned, whether the present position of the industry has been in any way improved. Stimulated by the demand for the products of flax which can no longer be procured in countries that were chiefly the source of supply prior to the war, the Government of the United States have inaugurated a live propaganda,. with a view to encouraging and developing flax culture in that country. It would seem that we in Canada would be neglecting our duty to ourselves, to the Empire and to the world, if at a time like this we did not awaken to the opportunities that now knock at our
doors by stimulating by every means within our power the development of flax culture and the production of fibre, and applying the fullest resources at our command to the study and means of making the best use of the various by-products which are incidental to the flax industry generally. As to how this may best be accomplished, there will be necessarily a difference of opinion, but that the whole subject is one that may well be considered by the Government through it's Department of Agriculture, who should be able to reconcile conflicting opinions and determine, in so far as the cultivation of the plant is concerned, just what is best to be done, I do not think any one in this House will doubt. But aside from this, there is a phase of the subject to which the Department Pf Trade and Commerce might well apply its energies. The Department of Agriculture can direct its efforts to the many problems necessary to the cultivation of the plant, the selection of seed, and possibly to the development of special seed suitable to the climatic and other conditions of this country. The department has rendered valuable aid in the matter of developing other cereals or seeds peculiarly suitable for our soil and climate. Though it is recognized that the best flax seed for sowing is imported from Holland, it may be that under experiments and with experience, our own Government may develop seed that will give better results in our country. It should be our aim to produce seed for the farmer that will give the best results, and that will assure the production of a fibre equal to the best that has been produced in those countries of Europe where for so many years the linen industries have not only given much employment to labour, but have also added much to their countries' productive wealth.
There are doubtless many prejudices in connection with the growth of flax. Farmers have an idea that its growth exhausts the soil, but the experiments carried on by the Department of Agriculture during the years 1906 to 1908, the results of which appear in Bulletin No. 59, show that this view is unwarranted. This bulletin asks: "Is flax a specially exhausting crop?" It answers this question as follows:
This question is usually .answered in the affl.mative, but this o inion does not app ar to be warranted by the chemical analyses which have been made of this crop, showing the principal elements of fertility taken from the



soil during the period of its growth. The results which have been obtained by chemical examination have furnished the following figures which represent approximately the plant food removed from the soil by flax, wheat and oats.
It is not necessary that I should give the figures, as the bulletin may be obtained by any one who makes application to the Department of Agriculture. Suffice to say that the summing up of the result is given thus:
It will be seen that the grain, in the case of the wheat crop, takes up a little more nitrogen and somewhat less of phosproric acid and potash than is taken by< the flax seed; while the oat crop takes for the grain a larger proportion of nitrogen, nearly one-third less of phosphoric acid and about one-eighth less of potash. The difference, however, in exhaustive effect of these several crops on a rich soil would scarcely be perceptible, and would not justify the opinion that flax is a very exhausting crop.
Notwithstanding these experiments made some eight years ago, it would seem desirable that the experimental farms should carry on investigations and furnish fullest information by bulletins to the farmers as to this matter. Doubtless with many farmers the prejudice is deeply rooted, and nothing bnt scientific experiments, which the Government can best carry out, and experience in results, will ultimately remove the objections which many farmers have to the growth of flax.
The United States have devoted a good deal of attention to investigations along the line of finding economic industrial use for the straw of flax, which is more essentially grown for the production of seed than of fibre, especially in those parts of the Western states, like our own Northwest, where the straw, instead of being returned to the soil, is burned. The result has shown that this straw as a by-product, may be utilized in many ways. From the paper-makers' standpoint, the flax crop represents a raw material of immense latent value, as it is likewise a source of great latent value to the farmer. In the United States, as in Canada, the seed flax of the West is different in type from that cultivated for fibre production, and because of this difference and of the methods of cultivating and handling the crop, the straw cannot be used to make a good spinning fibre. The straw resulting from the harvesting and threshing of this crop is usually burned, not because it has no intrinsic value, but because adequate industrial use has not been established to absorb it. A bulletin published by the United States Department of Agriculture dated January

7, last, reporting recent tests made on the utilization of seed flax straw in the paper and fibre board industry, states that successful commercial tests have been completed wherein domestic flax straw and tow were used in place of imported flax waste in the manufacture of fibre-board. The tests made were pronounced satisfactory and the product sold to the trade at the regular price for such boards. From an economic point, therefore, at a time when we are urged to conserve all the resources of our country, it would seem inconsistent that this country should waste its millions of tons of flax straw. Might it not be a subject worthy of the closest investigation of the Government to encourage the commercial use of this by-product?
Our acreage in flax in the year 1912 was equal to that of the United States in 1914. James L. Merrill, paper-plant chemist in the paper plant investigations of the United States Department of Agriculture referring to the waste of the straw of seed flax in that year, said that (1) its paper-producing possibilities would be equal to the annual production of wrapping paper, and more than double the annual production of writing paper in the United States; (2) its sale would represent, in add,ed revenue to the farmers, about $5,000,000 annually; (3) it would exert a very strong tendency towards maintaining the flax crop in our agricultural system; (4) it would probably result in the establishment of paper manufacturing industries where there are now none; (5) it would aid in making our paper industry more independent of foreign papermaking raw materials; and (6) it would produce a keener realization of the latent value of some of our enormous crop wastes. These investigations, which, have cost much in time and money, are surely worth 'the closest consideration of our Government, and they are in every sense as applicable to the conditions in Canada as 'to. those in the United States.
From every viewpoint the cultivation of flax would seem to mean, under proper conditions, more new-found wealth than the production of any other single plant. If it be possible-and some authorities agree that it is-to cultivate flax that will produce seed of best quality, and at the same time straw for fibre of high standard, much advancement will be made and the value of the crop greatly increased. Whether this be so or not, the prevailing opinion and custom in this country is to grow flax separately either for seed or for fibre. The

Northwest has produced flax primarily for seed, and so far little, if any, use has been made of the straw. In Ontario flax has been grown more for fibre, the proportion grown for that purpose last year being about four-fifths of the whole. The total value of the production of seed in Canada between the years 1910 and 1915, as per census of January, 1916, amounts to $87,933,000, so that the importance of flax growing to the agricultural industry is not inconsiderable.
The need of Government co-operation as a means to produce not only more, but better, flax has been demonstrated beyond any doubt. The Canadian Textile Journal, in its issue of September last, has an article contributed by Mr. Jas. A. McCracken, secretary of the Ontario Flax Growers' Association, who is probably in a position to speak with knowledge, in which he shows that in many respects t'he industry is groping in the dark, and needs the united cooperation of the Government in the propagation and production of a Canadian flax seed adapted to the peculiar needs of our climate and soils. In this article he says, among other things:
After close observation of the stanfls in various Helds of western Ontario and elsewhere for twenty years, I am a strong advocate of more particular grading and soil cultivation. Every fibre field I have ever seen produced a more or less uneven stand, more noticeably so than Helds of wheat, oats, or barley. This is the result of non-germinating seed, and the early death of many young plants from weak vitality. We certainly know too little about imported flax seed. We renew every two or three years. It comes to us from native conditions considerably different from ours. Most of it produces flax to be sure, but there are many failures of crop that seem attributable to nothing but the partial non-adaptability of foreign varieties to the soil and climatic conditions of Canada. There should be seed plots in this country where the talent and money required for seed breeding and development would be available. Our agricultural colleges are constantly evolving and creating new and excellent varieties of oats, wheat, barley and rye, but flax is practically neglected. No one man, especially now after a decade of depression, can finance this work successfully. It is a matter for combined effort and Government assistance. H. L. Bollry, botanist of the North Dakota Agricultural College, has shown what can be done in this direction by developing well-resistant seed and discovering that a spraying of formaldehyde makes the seed immune from exterior ravages by the spores of wilt and canker fungi. These are not vital considerations where fibre flax is grown ^on a studied rotation as in Ontario, but they show us what can be done by patient investigation and study.
The United States has a fibre bureau, which has been in operation for twenty-five years, working on flax, jute, hemp, and
other fibre-bearing plants adaptable to their climate. The Irish have special government flax bodies for the promotion of flax study, but Canada seems to be still in the dark in this respect, though it has been established beyond peradventure that flax for fibre can be produced in western Ontario of as good a quality as anywhere else on the globe.
Further, the Government having undertaken the task of developing a suitable Canadian, seed, may well further prosecute their investigations along the line of applied science and seek to determine the best methods to be employed in the production of tl>e fibre. Opinions . as regards this likewise vary. In many places, and generally throughout Ontario, it is still held that the old method of pulling the flax by hand is best. Against this the scarcity of labour has been a deterrent factor in the matter of greater production.. If experience and science demonstrate that those who hold to the view that pulling is the best method are right in their contention, then the ingenuity of man, and the aid of the Government, should be directed to the invention of machinery that would do this work with, economy of man labour, and to the cheapening of flax production. I understand that some advancement has already been made along these lines by the invention of Chas. H. Vessot, of Ottawa, and A. G. Mathers, who have produced a flax-pulling machine that in some measure meets the requirements and results in diminishing the cost of pulling by fifty per cent. Testimonials from prominent flax-growers in western Ontario bear testimony to the efficiency of the machine, and show that their experience has been that its use reduces the cost of pulling by from sixty to seventy-five per cent. By some it is claimed that this machine, while performing most effective and satisfactory work under certain conditions, is not yet so perfected that it will meet all conditions. It would there-* fore seem that Canadians have made considerable progress towards producing that which the ages heretofore have not yet, produced, a machine for pulling flax. Might not the" Government lend its aid to the further improvement and perfecting of this device? The Government could also materially assist in developing a process for the subsequent treatment of flax, which, while avoiding the difficulty of procuring cheap labour, would achieve the same -results as hand pulling. If such a system were worked out it should be possible to develop a large and important flax indus-

try which would take rank with the other great stable industries of Canada.
The proprietors of a mill at St. Catharines, Ontario, have for some years devoted much' time and investigation to this subject, and in their report on the subject the management say:
For several years past many machines have been devised and constructed and various improvements introduced having for their object the improvement of agricultural conditions- the. sowing, pulling and harvesting of the flax. These are all more or less successful and in time will be made entirely so, but the subsequent treatment of the straw and its conversion into fibre is the branch of the industry to which we have chiefly directed our efforts.
By the process which we have developed the hand pulling will be largely done away with, and the subsequent spreading in the field entirely eliminated. In future the flax will be brought direct from the field, threshed by specially designed threshing machines, and immediately baled by powerful hydraulic .process into bales each containing about 700 pounds of flax.
These bales are then carried by electric carriers or hoists and placed in large concrete tanks of a capacity of about ten tons of flax each. Here the flax is treated by means of bacteria cultures in water held constantly at the required temperature, by which means the flax is thoroughly " retted " in from two to three days.
From the tanks the wet flax is lifted by electric hoists and passed immediately to large specially constructed dryers, where in the short space of three hours the moisture is removed, leaving the flax thoroughly dry, and ready for the next operation.
From the dryer the bales are carried by overhead conveyors to the machinery room, where it is mechanically fed into large breakers ana the wood broken and crushed into fine particles, the fibre being carried automatically into large shakers or beaters, where it is thoroughly cleaned and the resultant fibre deposited into large bins ready for baling and shipment to the spinning mill.
From the above it will be seen that no experienced or expert labour is required. The process is short and inexpensive, Is positive in its results, and will produce a uniform grade of fibre. It can be done in any quantity desired. It is entirely free from weather conditions and can be carried on the whole year round and is not limited to a few weeks in the [DOT]'autumn as in the present system. Our mill is designed to handle 20 tons of straw per day, but additional mills can be erected and machinery installed capable of treating all the flax that can be grown in the entire country and as rapidly as the same can be produced by the farmers.
The object kept in view in designing and installing this plant for handling the flax has been simplicity and economy, and these two words are written large over the entire process ; from the harvesting of the flax right through to the baling and shipment of the fibre to the spinning mill, everything has been designed to handle the flax by the. most economical labour-saving methods so as to assure the farmer who grows the flax steady market for his product and at profitable prices, and also to insure our company in the opera-

tion of the plant a regular manufacturer's profit in producing the fibre for the trade.
It is now only a question of the intelligent co-operation of the Government with the farmers and flax producers to secure a sufficient quantity of flax-the raw material of the linen trade-in order to make possible the building up of a large and prosperous flax industry in the Dominion of Canada. It is simply a question of the production of the raw material and the investment of sufficient capital to manufacture the same into fibres, yarns and linens.
This firm, I understand, has been using this method with very satisfactory results, and it would seem that, as a result'of their experiments, a new era in the flax industry is about to dawn.
It would seem, therefore, that there is sufficient divergence of expert opinion to justify the Department of Agriculture in taking immediate steps to make a thorough investigation of the whole subject, and lending to agriculture and industry the aid of their practically limitless resources to solve the vexed problems that for years have been the stumbling block to success. The department might also take up the matter of utilization of the straw from flax grown, particularly for seed, by which as a byproduct at the present time is a
4 p.m. total waste, but which, under scientific use in applied industry, might become of economic value impossible now to conceive. Then there is the by-product of the flax, or I might say of the linseed mills,- the oil cake. This commodity, which is produced in considerable quantities as a necessity in the production of linseed oil>
is, I understand, a most valuable stock food, and yet only a limited proportion of what we produce is consumed by our stockmen. Does it not seem incongruous that, in a country like ours, with its millions of acres of grazing land, a country which beyond any other is peculiarly 'adapted to stock raising, this valuable by-product, linseed meal and oil cake, should be sent to Belgium, France, England, and other European countries to fatten and develop their live stock, and that our farmers, possibly for need of knowledge of its value as a feed to stock, do not avail themselves of its use. I say the Government can do much along the lines of conducting an educative campaign to correct these conditions, and to encourage the consumption, as far as may be necessary, amongst our stock rpen in Canada.	-
The Department of Agriculture, having applied itself to a solution of these problems, might not the industry be further encouraged by the Department of Trade and Commerce? Having produced our flax fibre, encouragement should be given to the

spinning of yarns in Canada, and this should be further followed by giving encouragement to the linen mills; otherwise, our country would receive only a small proportion of the productive value of the product, Fibre is the raw material of the spinning mill for years, and this yarn again is the raw material of the linen mill used in the manufacture of linens. It will appear that flax, developed to the limit of its possibilities, will produce a greater amount of increased wealth than any other plant grown; and therefore, in the words of my resolution, more attention should be given to promoting its cultivation in Canada, Both as to culture and manufacture, the industry should receive that aid and consideration from the Government which would enable it to assume the importance the natural resources of our country assure. In countries where its development has reached the highest stage, governments have appreciated its value and the need of government aid; and even in Great Britain, where bonuses and protection in the way of import duties are the direct antithesis of her economic policy, the need for granting bounties to encourage the production of flax in Ireland, was recognized as far back as 1911, and in a single year as much as $100,000 has been paid to producers in bonuses. Even here in Canada we have applied the principle of bounties to certain comodities. I find by the Trade and Commerce returns for the year ending March 31, 1914, that we paid in bounties a total sum

I say, therefore, it would not be inconsistent with the policy we have adopted towards other industries if we, like other countries, recognized the great importance to economic productiveness in giving to flax cultivation and flax fibre production most liberal aid, even if it implied liberal bounties to the farmers. If flax pulled is determined to be the best method of handling the crop, it would not be unreasonable to ask the Government to give a bounty on fibre production equal to at least half of the cost of the labour of pulling, which is said to be $8 per acre.
In France this policy has been and is now pursued. There they give a bounty of $5 per acre in cases where flax is pulled and utilized for its fibre. This policy has been fully justified, it would appear, from the resulting mammoth textile industries widely distributed throughout the northern, half of the country.
Ireland takes a different method, but an effective one, in stimulating flax culture. The Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction for Ireland has charge of flax education. A thorough course in flax culture and manufacture is given to students, and the young graduates are sent out over the country to spread the gospel of improved methods. Belgium, which for years back has been the home of the highest grades of flax products, is now devastated, and it might be possible, if the Government directed efforts to that end, to get a number of expert flax men from that country to come over to Canada and lend their aid and experience to communities in this country. A few of these men have already reached us, and can be found around districts in western Ontario such as Forest, Alvinston and Mitchell, and some have been engaged in flax mills in these districts. Around Wallaceburg there is a large colony of Belgians and Dutch. The fact that sugar beets and flax require attention at different periods of the growing season, together with the fact that both crops like best the same kind of soil, would encourage the hope that these industries might be developed side by side.
The possibilities for flax culture in this country are so great, and its economic value so immense, that I feel that our Government would fail in the discharge of their duty to agriculture and to productive wealth if they did not without further delay arouse themselves to the great need that confronts them with reference to this subject. The United States Year Book for 1913 shows that in that year Canada had under flax cultivation 1,553,000 acres of flax, and produced 17,539,000 bushels of seed, and the United States on an acreage of 2,291,000 acres produced only 17,853,000 bushels. The adaptability of our climate and soil would seem to far outrival that of the country to the south.
This subject is so important, Mr. Speaker, and the possibilities so immense, that the

discussion of it might be continued at some length. I feel that I have not only unduly trespassed on the patience of the House in presenting the facts that I have collected, though I must confess there is doubtless much that might be said concerning it that I have not said. In closing, I would just add that the grading of flax fibre, the sorting of it, and the establishing of standards would seem to be matters of importance, and should receive the consideration of the Government, as also co-operation in the marketing of the product.
The Secretary of the Canadian Flax Growers' Association has sent me a communication in which he outlines certain ideas and suggestions concerning a flax culture bureau. I do not wish to tire the House, but I would like to read this communication and to have it placed on reeoi'd as an expression of the views of a man who has had experience, and whose judgment is entitled to consideration:
Suggestions for Max Culture Bureau.
Arguments for its Creation.
Cotton interests have put flax into as much disfavour as possible. Canada can never become great in cotton. She can become great in flax. Flax cultivation has failed to advance and flax manufacture to succeed because the industry has never been boosted by big or influential organizations. Even the manufacturers of flax fibre are not united. Thus the educational propaganda necessary to place such an industry (embracing as it does many processes) on its feet and to overcome both the farmer's and the labourer's prejudice, has been lacking.
A single instance of successful fibre production in Canada justifies government encouragement, and support for the industry. Thousands of instances prove that first-class fibre can be produced in Canada.
The farmer's prejudice against flax is wholly unwarranted, as the experimental stations have proven. Flax, besides, is an enemy to the wire worm; flax entails a vigorous campaign against weeds.

The flax growers in the western part of Ontario, realizing their responsibility to the country, did their utmost to increase production last year; in fact, I doubt whether any other part of Canada made a more pronounced effort in that direction last year than the counties of Huron and Lambton. I know that my hon. friend the member for East Lambton (Mt. Mr. Speaker, I had not noticed this resolution on the Order Paper until my hon. friend from East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) moved it in the House this afternQon, or I should have given the matter some thought. I notice that he hopes the Government will give ''serious" encouragement. Did he mean to suggest that the Government do not as a rule give "serious" encouragement to the farmers of this country? Well, perhaps the word is appropriate under the circumstances. I wish that my hon. friend, instead of merely giving a resume of the flax industry, had brought down some cut-and-dried proposition that we could have fully discussed. We all know, of course, that the flax industry is a valuable one, and that there is lots of room for improvement in that industry in Canada. A few years ago there was a strong agitation for flax mills in this country for the purpose of making paper out of the flax straw

in the West, which at the present time is burned or thrown away. Nothing, however, came of that agitation because moneyed interests could not be induced to advance money for the project. I quite agree with my hon. friend that it would be an excellent idea for the Government to appoint some one who has a knowledge of the business, and general business ability, to look into the whole question with a view .to making recommendations to the Government. I am quite sure that there are men in the Agricultural Department capable of doing this work.
Among other things, my hon. friend read a statement to the effect that oil-cake and flaxseed meal are not much used in this country by the farmers, and the writer of the article wondered why these foodstuffs were not more used by farmers, instead of allowing them to be shipped to foreign countries. On behalf of the farmer let me say that the up-to-date fanner in this country calculates just how much protein and fats there are in every feed he gives. If oil-cake at' a certain price will pay him better than oats at a certain price, he will buy oil-cake; or he will buy oil-cake in preference to cottonseed-meal if it pays . him better. But if it does not pay him to use oil-cake, then, like the rest of us, he will not buy it. The farmer who is progressive and knows his business has things calculated pretty fine and knows just which food pays him best. Cottonseed-meal with - 41 per cent protein pays better at $40 a ton than oilcake at the same price with only 35 per cent protein. I think oilcake in places like Woodstock is sold at $40 a ton laid down, and cottonseed-meal at about $38; but cottonseed-meal contains more protein or butter fat, and the farmers are therefore buying it in preference to oilcake. I can say positively from my own experience that oilcake is a very excellent food, but at the same time if other countries will pay more for it than our farmers, it is only natural that the producers should ship it to the highest market. There is no doubt that the fibre could be made up entirely in this country. Speaking offhand, I would say that the Government might very well look into the question whether linen could be produced in Canada from the fibre, also paper, and at what cost. If it could be shown that the proposition would pay, there would be no trouble in getting people with means to go into the business. The
Government might very well investigate this question, and then lay before the House a definite proposition as to the amount of assistance required.
I have nothing more to say except to endorse my hon. friend's resolution so far as it goes, but I do not think it is definite enough. I hope the hon. member for Bast Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) will give us something more definite than a general resume of conditions of the flax industry throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to know that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is interested in this question and anxious to support the resolution. I agree with him that, instead of the words " serious encouragement," the words "immediate attention" should be inserted in the resolution, so as to make the resolution stronger. We must, however, qpngratulate the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) on the large amount of research he has made in gathering together the facts in regard to the flax industry and on the able manner in which he has presented them to the House.
This resolution deserves the attention of every hon. member, because practically every province in Canada is and has been deeply interested for many years in the flax industry, and when one takes into consideration the enormous production of flax seed and flax fibre or straw in Canada one will appreciate the fact that immediate attention should be given to the development of that- industry. I regret exceedingly that the serious accident which the Minister of Agriculture met with on the occasion of the fire in the parliament buildings prevents him being present. I cannot too highly congratulate the minister (Mr. Burrell) on what he has accomplished in past years, and while my remarks may appear to be somewhat of a criticism of the lack of interest or initiative shown by the Department of Agriculture in regard to the flax industry, I can assure you, Sir, that, in his administration of all the other branches of agriculture the minister is deserving of every consideration and confidence.
When war was declared, I called the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that the flax industry, in those countries that have for years been producing flax fibre in great quantities, was very much demoralized. I was able to show that France, Belgium and Germany, three of the large flax fibre producing countries, would for years to come be unable to produce the flax required for the linen mills of Ireland,

the United States and other countries. In the year previous to the war Russia had 3,500,000 acres under flax; but owing to the careless manner in which the flax industry is conducted there, the active men who are interested in the flax industry m Canada need not be afraid of that eom-petition.-
Last session, speaking in the House on the second day of March, I called the attention of the Government to the importance of investigating this question, to the need of immediate attention and assistance being given to our flax producing centres, and to the encouragement and education required for the development of the industry. I informed them that fifty years ago in the province of Ontario we had 80 flax fibre mills in operation; that forty years ago we had 65 mills; that twenty years ago we had 30 mills, and that two years ago we had only 9 flax mills. There must be good reasons for these mills going out of business, and I shall place before the Government some of these reasons, and point out the need of immediate attention being given to supplying a remedy. In Quebec, I believe that in Rouville there is one mill still in operation, and if my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) will look back at the history of the flax industry in his district, I am sure that he will appreciate my remarks and will support the resolution under discussion.
I have before me a map of the province of Ontario showing the districts in which flax mills were formerly located, the mills that are now in active operation, and those that have gone out of existence. The Department of Agriculture does not appear to give any assistance to this branch of agriculture, nor does it assist by experiments on its experimental farm its development. When one considers that in 1910, there were in the Dominion 476,000 acres under flax, 438,000 acres in Saskatchewan, 24,577 in Manitoba and 14,300 in Alberta, besides what was grown in Ontario and the other eastern provinces, we must realize the im-

portance of some active interest being taken towards the development of this industry by a branch of the Department of Agriculture which .should at once be organized for that purpose. We ought to have good seed for planting purposes so that we may increase the quality of the fibre. In 1911, in Western Canada, 1,500,000 tons of flax straw was burned, whereas if that had been turned into flax fibre it would be worth, at the prices current today, $100,000,000, and be it remembered that the farmers of the western provinces received only $11,555,000 for the seed which they produced.
As the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) has said: this is Canada's opportunity. Canada never can produce cotton, but she can become great in the production of flax, and there is no reason why every province of Canada should not assist in the development of this industry. Some years ago the Minister of Agriculture set aside $10,000,000 for the purpose of assisting in the education and development of agriculture throughout the various provinces, and if the Federal Government -are determined not to take an active interest in the flax industry, they should urge upon the Provincial Governments the need of expending some of the money that is handed over to them out of this fund towards that end.
