I said that every province was interested in this proposition. We are not here today asking for a bonus, or a duty, but we-are here asking that some definite proposition should be presented as a result of which this industry could be developed along proper lines. Before I sit down I shall try and carry out the wishes of the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) by placing before the House a definite proposition. All that we are asking for is education and experiment. Go to the experimental farms in every province of this country and you will find that they are paying little or no attention to experimental work in connection with the flax industry. It is true that some little attention was given to it last fall. Mir. Grisdale went to Washington, and some slight efforts have been made towards inquiring into the needs of the industry. But I do not feel

that we should lose valuable time, especially when the market for the product is calling for enormous quantities of it at prices double what they were a few years ago and which should bring very great returns to the millers and farmers. In western Ohtario, in 1913, we had 2,500 acres under flax for fibre; in 1914 we had 1,300 acres, and in 1915, 4,000 acres. Our mills have increased in number until last year we had 27 in operation, largely in that western district.
How much of the flax was grown in Lambton?
We have five mills in operation in Lambton.
How many acres of flax were grown in Lambton?

I would be afraid to estimate. The mills have increased in the last two years from 9 to 27 in the province of Ontario, and there are ten new mills that are to be opened during the present spring. I am satisfied that if a reasonably earnest effort were put forth a large number of these mills could be opened in different parts of our province, and in the eastern and western provinces as well.
I listened to the hon. member for East Middlesex while he was calling attention to the fact that foreign countries bonus and assist this industry in many ways. Surely it is a reasonable request for us to make that at least an educational campaign should be carried on looking to the development of this industry. In Russia they have established ten standards of flax fibre.
In Canada we have no -such thing as a standard for flax. Our millers are carrying on their industry by guesswork largely, sending their product abroad and receiving what little they can for it, while, as a matter of fact, they should be furnished with all kinds of information in regard to the markets for the disposal of this product and to assist them in the development of the industry. My hon. friend from East Middlesex called attention to what Ireland; through the Board of Agriculture, is doing for the development of the flax industry. Surely that is worthy of our consideration. In Australia the mills are assisted and an export fibre bonus is paid. Experiments should be carried on in all experimental farms; factories should be furnished with proper asistanoe and information in regard to the handling of the product, and the 
farmers should be educated by the distribution of pamphlets and of general information regarding the caTe of the product and the harvesting of the crop.
I believe that a division under the Experimental Farm Branch of the Department of Agriculture should be opened immediately, similar to the live stock division, field husbandry division, serialists division, forage crop division, horticulture division, poultry division, botany division and chemistry division.
The duties connected with this division should cover the sending out of literature from time to time to men interested in flax growing and production. The districts where mills are not now being operated should be visited, and if possible the owner should be induced to re-open these mills. Information and encouragement should be given the owners in the way of securing proper seed and giving encouragement to the farmers of the district. The flax mills in operation should be visited by experts at times of seeding, harvesting, spreading, retting -and turning, in order that the best results might be obtained. The person in charge of the division should see that the best seed is used for planting purposes. Proper grading of_flax fibre for export should be carried on. He should investigate the new means of retting and pulling which are being introduced from time to time. The miller should be kept posted in the latest European and American methods of handling the flax. Ways and means should be found for the disposing of flax and its by-products in Canada and in foreign lands. The flax grower should be assisted in importing the proper kind of flax-seed from Holland or elsewhere, and co-operation should be encouraged. The division should aim at the standardization of flax both as to seed and fibre. New Canadian strains should be developed. Encouragement should be given in the way of baling the crop, and information sent out concerning tests as to the exhaustiveness of flax on the soil.
Lower freight rates should be secured. The western provinces should be visited and a thorough investigation made into the methods of growing flax and the possibility of using the straw or fibre for export or milling purposes. The United States, Ireland, Holland, France and other countries should be visited and their methods of growing and curing the product carefully inquired into and studied. The districts located in the provinces of Quebec

and Ontario, where flax is now being produced, should be visited at the earliest possible date, and every encouragement given to the millers and farmers to become interested in the development of the flax industry. I appeal to the members of this House to give this matter their earnest consideration, and to the Government to take immediate action to secure the development of this industry in Canada along proper lines.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we
have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the mover (Mr. Glass) and the seconder (Mr. J. E. Armstrong) of this resolution affecting what is in some parts of the world a great industry.
I was interested in the remarks of the seconder of the resolution with regard to flax growing in Canada. The fact that fifty years ago 80 mills were in operation in Canada-largely, I think, in the province of Ontario-forty years ago, 65; twenty years ago, 30; two years ago, 9, shows that considerable experimenting has already been carried out in connection with flax-growing in this country. I happen to come from a part of the country where some of this experimenting has been carried on. While I may not be altogether in accord with some of the views expressed by the mover and the seconder of this resolution, I do not want it to be understood that I am not in favour of all possible light being thrown upon the subject. I was impressed with the remark of the mover of the resolution to the effect that the views which he expressed were based upon his own observations. There are two sides to the question. I believe that the prejudice of the farmers against flax production, referred to by the secretary of the Flax Growers' Association, is not unnatural. While the growing of flax . in Canada since the beginning of the war has proved unusually profitable, by reason of the good prices received for the fibre, yet, having regard to the agricultural condition of the districts where flaxgrowing was extensively carried on for a number	of	years,	I for	one
do not look favourably upon the encouragement of the industry. In the harvesting of a flax crop the whole plant is taken from the soil, even the root. It is said that machinery has been invented whereby fldx may be cut and harvested like other grain. To my knowledge, however, that experiment was made thirty-five or forty years ago, and the objection was that the very best of the fibre was left on the field. When you think of the fight that the farmer is continually
waging against noxious weeds, you will appreciate the difficulties that he has to contend with in growing a crop of flax. The whole crop has to be pulled; this operation involves a good deal of labour. In western Ontario I believe the custom has been to get large numbers of Indians from the reserves to camp in the flax-growing districts and pull the flax. The flax was stuked up on the land, and as it remained there for a considerable period, the farmer was unable to cultivate the land immediately after harvest. All the weeds that grew in the crop, being left on the soil seeded there, and in a short time the land became impoverished and full of weeds. Farmers who engaged in flax-growing for a number of years were eventually driven out of the business for that reason. Of my own personal knowledge, I know of farms that were rendered practically useless for any other purpose simply because flax was grown upon them for a number of years, and only after many years were they restored to a reasonable state of productivity. I do not know so much about the condition in western Canada, but I am satisfied that with the new lands they have there, they can grow great crops of flax. I doubt very much, however, whether their climatic conditions will permit them to rett the flax so that they can separate the wood from the fibre. In western Ontario the conditions in the fall of the year are different from what they are in Western Canada. If you look over the records I believe you will find that flax growing is popular only in countries where they have cheap labour. I believe that India is the largest flax-producing country in the world. Argentina is second, and Russia third. United States is a large grower of flax, but she does not engage in the industry as these other countries do. The labour conditions in Canada make it very difficult in normal times to grow flax at a profit. I am satisfied that the farmers of western Ontario would make a great mistake if they should change their system of agriculture and go into the growing of flax, which entails a great drain on the land, whose fertility can be maintained only by the usq of artificial fertilizers. I am satisfied that agriculture must be carried on more scientifically in Canada in the future than has been the case in the past. In Ontario, in years gone by, when there was a great deal of new land, flax was a splendid crop to sow on the land the first two or three crops, while rotting the sod, levelling the soil, and bring-

ing it under a system of cultivation. And I believe that even to-day in those sections where mills have been re-erected, the prevailing custom is to sow flax on sod with a view to rotting the sod. But I am afraid of the consequences and I would not like to advise the Government to encourage the growth of flax in this country. A few years ago, I believe, a certain association claimed that they were able to separate the fibre of flax without rotting it. The unrotted flax fibre was going to revolutionize the whole system of flax growing, not only in Canada but in the world. If that were the case, probably in Western Canada it would be a great boon to that country, because I have no doubt that with the system of farming they are able to carry on there, with a rich, virgin soil which will undoubtedly stand cropping for a number of years, they could make it a very profitable enterprise. I have my doubts as to the possibility of making that industry a success in Ontario, particularly in those districts where they have had considerable experience in the growing of flax. ' I have fresh in my mind the scene that meets my eye every year when the grain is maturing and when I pass through those districts in which flax used to be grown quite a number of years ago. You find that in those fields, even to-day, it has been impossible to obliterate the effects of growing flax. The fields in those districts .are as yellow as gold with the wild, mustard that grows in the soil as a result of the cultivation of flax. I believe that the weed nuisance, if I am not permitted to describe it by a more severe name than that, is the greatest enemy the farmers of Canada have to contend with to-day, and that it is costing this country annually hundreds of millions of dollars. I believe that the Government will have to resort to drastic measures in order to stop the spread of noxious weeds. It must not be longer tolerated. I do not wish to couple these objections with this resolution, but the two are so bound up, in my mind, that I can scarcely separate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How has the growing of flax caused' the spread of wild mustard?

For the reason I pointed out, that it is almost impossible to pull weeds among flax without tramping it down arid destroying the crop. With other crops you can go through and pull out what mustard there is in the field, but you cannot do that with flax. The mustard matures and the seed spreads on the ground

before the flax is ripe. The same thing is true of other weeds.

How is it that in western Ontario, where we have the oldest-established flax mills, which have been in continuous operation for many years, the farmers in the districts convenient to them are the most successful farmers in the country?

In my boyhood days, which is a considerable time ago, we had three mills in the county in which I live, and for the last 15 or 20 years there has not been a mill in operation there. I understood from the remarks made by the hon. member for East Lambton that 50 years ago there were 80 mills, 40 years ago about 45 mills, 20 years about 30 mills, and 2 years ago only 9 mills in Canada. I think that is a sufficient answer to the question.
Is there not a mill at Tavistock?
Tavistock is partly in Perth Comity. I am not sure whether the mill is on our side of the line or not.
It is on our side.

Some time ago I, in common with other members of this House, received a letter - from Mr. Fraleigh regarding the giving of some consideration by the Government to the flax growers of Ontario. I think this question aifects the western part -of the province to a greater degree than any other part. I cannot, with my knowledge of the subject, go into details as other gentlemen have done, but from hearing the figures given to-day and from reading the circular to which I have referred, the subject appeals to me in this way, that if there is the large acreage growing flax which has been quoted by the hon. member for East Lamb-ton, and if the mills have gradually fallen off from their former prosperity, and if, as the flax growers seem to think, the growing of flax, if properly attended to and with sufficient co-operation between the Department of Agriculture and the growers, is a profitable business it is a fit and proper case for the favourable consideration of the Government and the demands of the flax growers ought to be acceded to, because they are simple demands. They say, in their circular, simply that they desire more co-operation as between the experimental farms and such institutions and the flax growers. Even if the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Suther-

land) is correct in the statement that the sowing and reaping of flax is liable to leave more weeds in the ground than the 'sowing of other grains, then there would seem to be even greater need for the Department [DOT]of Agriculture stepping in and finding out if that state of affairs actually exists, so that the farmers and those interested in the growing of flax may know whether they are sowing a crop that it is advantageous for them to grow. I only desire to repeat that with the acreage sown to flax and the extent of the industry in western Ontario, it appears to be a proper case for the consideration of the Government. If they are not receiving sufficient consideration from the Government and the Department of Agriculture, surely the department should undertake such experiments as will satisfy those interested in the industry that everything is being done that will be of advantage. If the result of these experiments proves that it is not a desirable industry, the flax growers should be told that. The whole matter seems to be in an experimental stage. Then surely it is the duty of the Department of Agriculture to make exhaustive experiments, and so the Government might well accede to the request made by the flax growers.

Mr. Speaker, judging by tile figures that have been given by hon. gentlemen opposite, it [DOT]vuuld appear that, during the past few years, the principal acreage of flax has been grown ;n the West, more particularly in the Province of Saskatchewan. As hon. members are aware, some years ago the price of flax was very high. At one time the farmers got, I think, as much as $2.25 per bushel; I know it was around $2 a bushel for a considerable period, and during those years a great deal of flax was grown. As was pointed out by one hon. member, we have never made any use whatever of the straw on the prairies; it has been used either for feeding, or has been burned, which ever was most convinient, I imagine, for the farmers. The money they made out of it, w.as altogether out of the seed. Anything done by the Government in the way of carrying out the wishes ' of the flax growers of Ontario, or of ascertaining whether the flax grown in the West is of the right quality to make a valuable fibre that will be worth money on the market, would I think be a step in the right direction. I certainly think it is the duty of the Government to take some steps, for after all it would be a simple matter to make the necessary experiments.
I know that a few years ago a company, having its head office in the Old Country and .a branch here, made some experiments, and tried to do something in the way of establishing mills throughout the West.
Their purpose was, as I was 5 p.m. informed, to pay-the farmers so much for the flax straw, after it came from the threshing mill, or so much an acre for the flax straw unthreshed; in fact, to cover both the grain and the straw. So far as I am aware, however, nothing was accomplished in that direction. Among the things that would help the flax industry in the West, there is one which I noticed that my hon. friend who moved the resolution (Mr. Glass) and the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) did not include.
I refer to the removal of the duty on flax going into the United States. So far as the flax in the West is concerned, Duluth is the principal market. We cannot consume the flax grown in our country, at least not a very large portion of it; we have to export it. A few years ago when the price was high, a duty of 25 cents a bushel, though a large tax, did not interfere with the growing of the flax, hut when the price went ' down, as it did a year ago, to something around $1 a bushel, a duty of 15 cents on flax going into the United States was quite enough to keep some farmers from growing flax to any extent. I would suggest that if the Government could secure the abolition of the duty on flax going into the United States they would probably do more than could be accomplished in any other way to encourage the growth of flax on the prairies. I think it would be better to adopt a system by which the straw could be used for mercantile purposes, but in the West I do not know that that idea would ever take a very great hold, because labour is high, the farms are large, and the settlements are thin and scattered. They would have to draw the straw a considerable distance, I imagine, in order to have it treated, but whether that would be the case or not I do not know. What I am sure of is, that something ought to be done by the way ol experiment, and I think the resolution moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Glass) is in the right direction. I trust that the Department of Agriculture will take hold of the question, find out something about it, and give the House the result of their investigations at an early date.

The views just expressed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) are very much in accord with those held by myself.

In the southern part of Alberta there is a considerable acreage of flax, not so much in recent years as formerly, and I am sure that if there was more encouragement for the use of the by-products of flax, there would be a greater acreage in that part of Western Canada. Flax grows there with a great deal of success, and the farmers are anxious to find some use for the flax straw.	They would also like to get
a much higher price for the flax if that could be secured. The flax straw problem has been discussed by the Board of Trade of the city of Lethbridge, and I understand that a few years ago a gentleman from Holland or Belgium travelled through the western country with the idea of establishing a factory for the purpose of utilizing this straw. I think that the Department of Agriculture should give every encouragement to experiments along that line. We are going into intensive farming more and more, and we do not want to waste anything. At the present time flax straw is being wasted, throughout Western Canada at any rate. It is of use in other countries, and we should ascertain whether it is not practicable to use it in this country so that the farmers may get full value for the flax which they grow.

I think that one of the reasons why farmers do not go in for growing flax is the excessive cost of threshing and marketing it. This applies perhaps more particularly to the great western country where there is a very large quantity of farm weeds. While threshing operations are in progress with regard to larger grains, such as wheat and oats, it is a comparatively easy matter to separate the weed seeds from the grain, but when you try to separate them from flax, you find it a much more difficult proposition. The result generally is that a certain percentage of those small weed seeds find their way into the flax when it is threshed, and a very large deduction has to be made when the farmer comes to sell it. Even the cleanest growers of flax have to face a reduction of 15 per cent when they sell the flax; that is, that amount is deducted by the elevator companies from the quantity the growers may happen to have in the oar. Then, as the hon. member for Assmiboia mentioned, the price cuts a considerable figure, the threshing of flax costs a good deal in the West. I have known 25 cents per bushel to be charged for simply threshing the flax; 20 cents per bushel is a very common charge in the West. The thresher will

thresh oats for perhaps 6 cents a bushel, and wheat for from 8 to 10 cents per bushel, according to the manner in which the threshing is done. The fact, therefore, that the cost of threshing flax is so much higher than that of threshing wheat or oats, that the- deductions are so much greater, and that there is difficulty in getting the whole crop to ripen at the same time so as to enable the grower to eliminate the immature seeds, all militate against the farmer in the growing of flax. The result has been that a good many farmers in the West, who would otherwise have made a success of it, have given up growing flax.
Perhaps under better conditions this might be made a more profitable crop. The farmers in the West say that they can get a crop of flax off land that would not be a success in growing wheat or oats, and a great deal of the flax of the West is produced under those conditions. As regards the province of Ontario, the people in the district from which I come go in for growing flax in only a very limited way indeed. I should be very pleased to see the Government take this matter up, and see whether something could not be done in the direction of utilizing flax straw. It is a question, I think, that comes very properly within the purview of this Government. Men have visited this Parliament in past years, bringing plans with them, and claiming that they had machines that would pull flax successfully; they said they had some process by which flax could be made mer-chantably profitable _ But as to all these things, our farmers are in very great doubt indeed, and I do not think it would involve any great expense if the Government put some of these processes to the test, in order to find out whether there was any hope of making a success of the flax industry in this country. If some way could be found of utilizing the straw in our great western country, it would certainly be worth while. Flax straw is cut up very much finer than ordinary straw in threshing, and the thought has sometimes occurred to me that perhaps flax straw could be compressed into bricks and used for fuel, like we use peat in the East. There have been in the West experiments with the burning of straw in large ovens or stoves, and the waste in the burning of the straw has been to some small extent utilized; at all events, attempts have been made to utilize it. Any one who is accustomed to growing flax in the West knows that it gives off an immense heat when fired, and I think there is a great

deal of this kind of heat stored up in the West. I should like to see this suggestion tested out, along with any other tests the Government may make when they take hold of this question.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The resolution
proposed by the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) opens up a question which I think is of very great importance and of very great interest as well. At the outset I may say that I can see no objection whatever to the adoption of the resolution, with this exception: the resolution suggests that " aid " should be given. It says:
That the flax and linen industries should, both as to culture and manufacture, receive that aid and consideration from the Government, which would enable it to assume the importance the natural resources of our country assuj'e it.
And in speaking to his resolution the hon. member for Middlesex also suggested that it might be desirable for the Government to give a bonus to encourage the flax industry. I do not wish any misapprehension to exist on that point. I do not think the House wishes it to be understood that in voting for this resolution they are voting for a resolution which contemplates giving a bonus for the encouragement of this particular industry. The word " aid " might possibly give the impression that financial aid was intended, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that " aid " be eliminated, and the word " encouragement " substituted therefor. I do not think it is the intension of the House to pass a resolution at the present time giving financial aid to this industry, but if that was the intention of the hon. member for Middlesex, I might point out that such a resolution could not properly emanate from a private member, by reason of the rule that resolutions involving money grants must emanate from a member of the Government. I therefore suggest that the word "aid" be struck out and the word "encouragement" be substituted therefor. The matter which my hon. friend has brought to the attention of the House, like all other matters affecting the agricultural industry of this country, is of great importance, and anything that can be done to encourage the farmers of this country to go into an industry that will be of advantage to them will be of very great value to the country generally. The flax industry in Canada to-day, as appears from the figures of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), is not a small industry. The value
of the flax produced last year in Canada, as my hon. friend has pointed out, amounted to $15,965,000-a very considerable amount, but very small in comparison with the value of the flax that could be produced in Canada if it was thought desirable, in the interests of the farmers and in the public interests, that more should be produced. Of that $15,965,000 worth of flax, over $13,592,000 was produced in the province of Saskatchewan alone. Of the balance, $1,675,000 was produced in Alberta, $576,000 in Manitoba, $107,000 in Ontario, and $15,000 in Quebec; while in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia no flax at all was produced. The $13,592,000 of flax that was produced in Saskatchewan was grown on 9,061,000 acres, and I believe that the great portion of that flax was grown, not for the purpose of producing fibre for making textiles and linens, but for the seed, out of which oil is made for feed for cattle. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has pointed out that there is not a large enough market in Canada for the production of a large quantity of flax, and that it might be of some assistance to the flax producer of this country if the United States Government removed the duty on flax. 1 might say to my hon. friend that so far as the production of flax for the manufacture of oil is concerned, there is a very great demand in Canada to-day for a much larger production. The paint makers of this country have been in communication with the Department of Agriculture about it, and have represented that the demand amongst the paint makers of this country to-day for the oil produced from flax seed is very much in excess of the supply in Canada at the present time. Not only is that the case in Canada, but there is also in Great Britain to-day a very large demand for linseed oil, and if the acreage in Western Canada was increased to a very great extent over what it is now, there would still be a market in Great Britain and Canada for all the oil that could be produced from the extra amount of flaxseed grown. I think my hon. friend, had more in mind, as the hon. member for Lambton had, than the growing of flax for the purpose of fibre out of which textiles could be produced. I speak without any practical knowledge of the subject, and only with such information as I have been able to obtain from reading, and in discussion with others, but I think I am correct in stating that the variety of flax from

which seed is produced for the purpose of oil, is not the best sort for the production of fibre out of which textiles can be manufactured. There is a difference in the quality and, to some extent, in the nature of the flax that is used for these different purposes. I might say the Department of Agriculture has been taking steps along the lines which have been suggested in the debate this afternoon, and I trust they will be of such a character as to satisfy the farmers of this country as to the advantage or disadvantage of raising flax in Canada. As was pointed out by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), who addressed the House some time ago, there is an apparent difference of opinion with regard to this matter. In certain parts of the country where farmers have ceased producing crops that at one time they produced, they have done so because, being alive to their own interests, they concluded that other crops would pay them better. This may be the^ reason why the farmers of Ontario are at the present time producing less flax than they did fifty years ago when the industry was, according to the figures given to-day by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), quite a flourishing one; but I know of sections in the eastern part of Canada where years ago the people produced a considerable quantity of wheat and where now they have altogether abandoned its production, finding it more profitable to purchase their flour from the millers of Western Canada and to use their lands for the production of crops of an entirely different character. Yet I have known of a case where, years later, under altered circumstances and conditions, farmers have returned to producing those crops which at one time they thought it was better to abandon in order to produce other crops that were more profitable, and that could perhaps be produced more easily. The same conditions may apply to the production of flax in Ontario. When the farmers of Ontario abandoned the production of flax to the extent stated by the hon. member for East Lambton the conditions may have been very different from those prevailing to-day, and, in the section of country from which my hon. friend comes, the farmers are evidently finding it to their advantage to return to the production of flax, because, if I understand my hon. friend aright, where two years ago there were only nine mills, there are now twenty-seven mills and ten more mills will be added during the present year. I conclude that the farmers, who are pretty 
good judges of their own interest and. who are practical men, have, at least in that portion of western Ontario in which the Lambtons and the Middlesexes are situated, decided that under the conditions that exist to-day it will pay them to raise flax, and consequently farms are being planted with flax and mills are being erected for the purpose of retting and scutching the flax after it is produced.
My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has referred to the fact that flax is not regarded as a desirable crop because of the difficulty of doing away with and destroying the weeds that grow amongst it, and because in pulling up the weeds, the fibre of the flax is apt to be destroyed, since, if I understand the flax business correctly, flax cannot be mowed or harvested as can wheat and oats. It has to be pulled up by the roots, because some of the very best part of the fibre is contained in the root, and if the flax is cut off by a mower or a reaper, a great deal of this very best part is wasted. Thus, in pulling up mustard weeds, which grow amongst the flax, there is danger of pulling the flax up and destroying the fibre and to a great extent destroying the crop. That is a matter that should be considered by the experts of the Department of Agriculture; and it is altogether likely that if experts n the culture of flax and experts in the experimental farm work take the matter up, they will be able to find a remedy for this trouble. At the present time the people interested in the flax business are endeavouring to find a remedy by the invention of machinery for the purpose of pulling up the flax so that the labour problem may be overcome, and the work of pulling not so expensive as it has hitherto been. I have before me the photograph of a machine invented for pulling the flax, which, if successful, will very much lessen the cost of pulling.
I have stated that the Department of Agriculture has taken this matter into its serious consideration. Mr. Grisdale, director of Dominion Experimental Farms, was some time ago directed by the Minister of Agriculture to look thoroughly into this matter with a view of working along the broad lines .suggested in the resolution now before the House. The result has been that the growing of flax for fibre has. during the past year, received very considerable attention from the department. A quantity of flax has been grown on the Ottawa Experimental Farm, and

there have been collected in the various provinces where, flax is grown, samples which have been retted here and scutched at Forest, Ontario. For the information of hon. members who perhaps know very little about the flax business, I may say that "retting" simply means "rotting," and is spelled with an "e" instead of an "o." This process is generally ftarried out by placing the pulled flax, or what we might call the straw, in water, and allowing it to remain for four or five days. At the end of that time the ligneous matter is retted or rotted to some extent and separated from the fibre. The mass is then taken out of the water and allowed, to dry, when it becomes quite brittle. It is then put through corrugated rollers and broken up. The next step in the treatment of the flax is the scutching. The scutching machine consists of an instrument something like a wagon wheel with the felloes removed and seven or eight spokes left attached to the hub. This is rolled over the straw, and by this means the woody portion is knocked off and the fibre is left. The fibre, as we have it in Canada, is something like.the sample that I have in my hand, and it is not manufactured into linen in this country, but is shipped, in this condition. This work has been going on at the experimental farm', and some very good samples have been obtained by means of this process.
In August last Mr. Grisdale, director of Dominion Experimental Farms, made a general investigation into the status of the industry and the possibility of its expansion in Canada. A bulletin on the subject of flax for fibre in Canada has just been prepared, and when printed it will be distributed generally amongst prospective flax growers. Mr. Grisdale has made a report on the subject, from which I will quote a few extracts:
Acting under instructions from the Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Martin Burrell, the writer has, during the last two or three weeks, made an effort to learn something about the " flax fibre " producing industry in Canada and the United States as to (1) information available in Government bureaus, (2) men capable of taking part in the propaganda to increase production and encourage the industry in Canada and available for such a purpose, (3) the line such a propaganda might follow, (4) the present state of flax for the fibre producing industry in Canada and the United States, and
(5)	general information on the subject.
For this purpose Mr. Grisdale first of all went to Washington to see what information he could get there from the secretary of the fibre division of the United States Bureau which is connected with the
Department of Agriculture of the United States. His visit there, however, showed him that very little information of real value had been collected by that division. The files showed but a,very small knowledge of people interested in the actual production of flax for fibre in the United States, and Mr. Grisdale found that the two men apparently recognized as the best men in the industry in the United States were Mr. B. Summers of the Summers Linen company, Port Huron, Mich., and Mr. Mc-Caul, of the James Livingstone Flax company, Yale, Mich., while in Canada the only man recognized as an authority was Mr. G. Howard Fraleigh,. of Forest, Ontario. Mr. Grisdale proceeded from Washington to Chicago, where he had an interview with Mr. Dewey, who, I understand, is connected with the Department of Agriculture at Washington, but who was not in Washington at the time of Mr. Grisdale's visit. Mr. Grisdale, in his report, states
Through kindness of Mr. Taylor, I was able to get into touch with Mr. Dewey by telegraph and to make an engagement to meet him in Chicago. This I did and found Mr. Dewey very sympathic in his attitude towards our efforts to gain information along various lines of interest in connection with fibre flax. He admitted, howeter, that neither he nor Mr. Miles, his assistant, was in a position to help us out although he expressed willingness to do anything he could in that way. Their knowledge was, he admitted, theoretical, rather than practical and the bulletin recently prepared by Mr. Miles was largely of the nature of a compilation rather than a work based upon results of practical work done by their division. The work being carried on by the fibre division with flax is along the following lines:
(a)	Improvement of varieties by selection from experimental plots being grown in the United States and by importation of new varieties. Blue and white blossom varieties are being tried out from seed imported from Russia, Belgium and Ireland.
(b)	Study of cultural .methods on farms in various parts of Michigan and Wisconsin.
(c)	Study of machinery and manufacturing methods.
(d)	Study of the fertilizers and soil requirements of the crop.
(e)	Dissemination through the medium of bulletins and leaflets of information collected.
Mr. Dewey corroborated what I had learned at Washington as to Summers, MeCaul and Fraleigh being the best men in America from the flax-for-fibre producers standpoint.
Heaving Chicago, I next visited Mr. Bartrand
S.	Summers, of the Summers Linen Co., Port Huron, Michigan, and was by him shown all through the rather extensive plant of this company. In this plant I was so fortunate as to see every operation under way except the threshing.
This company-which is really Mr. Summers 

is the only firm known to carry on chemical retting on a commercial scale in the flax world. The threshed flax is baled and brought in from as far as 25 or 30 miles in box cars. It is



retted in a large steel cylinder, probably 20 feet long by 10 feet in diameter, lying on its side and having two port holes with iron doors on top. It will ret about 5 tons at one time.
In Mr. Summers5 opinion the most serious problems confronting the growers of flax for fibre to-day are: (1-) better varieties, (2) better cultural methods, (3) a pulling machine, (4) better fertilizing methods, (5) more information on best time to harvest, (6) a scutching machine.
He considers that if a puller could be perfected a tremendous advance will have been made in the industry in America and that fibre flax would immediately take a prominent place among crops over very considerable areas in Canada and the United States. He considers climatic and soil conditions over practically the whole of western Ontario as highly suitable for production of fibre flax.
Mr. Summers has built a flax puller which has given fairly good results and he thinks that he may yet be able to make a really first class machine of this kind. Mr. Fraleigh, of Forest, Ont., with whom I discussed this machine seems to think that Mr. Summers would eventually have a really good puller. Mr. Summers has also built a scutching machine which he showed me, but he did not seem particularly optimistic as to its future, admitting that: it was far from perfect yet.
Mr. Summers did for some years manufacture rugs from a certain proportion of his output of fibre. These rugs so'd well and wear well. He has, however, been forced to abandon the manufacture for the present on account of a fire in his factory and the scarcity of suitable dyes since the beginning of the war. Mr. Summers imports seed from Holland and Russia and also from Canada. From Holland he gets the best seed from Mr. Lucard-e, of Rotterdam. Mr. Summers claims to have found a market for a part at least of the ligneous residues from scutching. It is to be used by a certain company as a base for a stock food.
Mr. Summers advised me that the best man in the business of producing flax for fibre today in America was Mr. G. Howard Fraleigh, Forest, Ont. So, on leaving Port Huron, I crossed to Sarnia thence to Forest and there met Mr. Fraleigh already mentioned several times above.
Mr. Fraleigh I found to be an enthusiastic and energetic grower of " flax for fibre He has been in the business some twenty odd years and seems to have made a decided success financially. He handles about 500 acres of flax for fibre each year. His plan of operation is. he states, practically the same as is followed all over Ontario and in Michigan. He rents fields of varying size from farmers in a radius usually of 5 or 6 miles but occasionally farther afield. The soil preferred is heavy loam, clay loam, or clay. Sometimes fields of lighter soil are selected but this kind of land is not favoured since the crop is more likely to suffer from drought in the early part of the season and so be short in the staple. The farmer undertakes to plough the land, at the time approximately indicated by the operator, disc-harrow, roll and harrow until ready for the seeder. Once the field is ready to sow the responsibility and the work of the farmer cease.
The report is a very interesting one, and will well repay the careful perusal of any member of the House interested in this and other agricultural subjects, but I cannot

trespass upon the time of the House by reading very much from it.
Mr. Fraleigh states that the industry of flax growing for fibre production in Ontario is at present in rather had shape for the reason, as he thinks, that the business has to some considerable extent got into the hands of promoters and others having no practical knowledge on the subject or at best very small experience. This is due to the fact that no new blood has been coming into the practical side of the business for some years and that recently the old men have been dropping out. Their business, where not allowed to go down, has usually been taken hold of by a promoter who has seen in it a chance to make money and is now using all the devices or schemes of the promoter to make it go and to make as much money out of it for himself as he possibly can. He claims that the old line men and the new men or promoters have little in common.
In the opinion of Mr. Fraleigh, as expressed to me, the thing that would do the most good to the industry in Canada would be the appointment of a man, who could immediately go out and help the producers by showing them how to grade their fibre products. Lack of proper grading methods results, he claims, in the loss of many thousands of dollars each year in Ontario. Such a man might also do something to help the industry by visiting the farmers and giving personal advice and also by getting out instructive literature.
The above report summarizes as briefly as possible such of the information I have been able to gather on the subject of flax for fibre production in Canada and the United States, as seems to me to be of sufficient importance to justify its incorporation herein.
The impression left upon me by all I have been able to see, and by the men I have had a chance to interview, I shall attempt to summarize in the following few sentences:
1.	Flax for fibre production in the United States is quite a negligible industry. It is confined almost entirely to Michigan and includes, I am reputably informed, not over five operators. The most important of these are the Summers Linen Co., Port Huron, Mich, and the Jas. Livingstone Flax Mills, Yale, Mich. Recent failures in various parts of the United States in this industry due to wrong methods- due to promoters-would seem to indicate no expansion in the near future.
2.	The Fibre Investigation Division of the bureau of Plant Industry, Washington, has carried on very little investigational work with flax and is not in a position to assist Canada with either information or men capable of collecting or imparting information on the subject.
3.	The Industry in Canada, while apparently profitable is in the hands of a very few people. There would seem to be room for a very considerable expansion.
4.	Prices for fibre .are high. The districts in Russia, Belgium and France where flax for fibre is grown most extensively are being devastated by the present great war. In some cases a large percentage of the men and other labourers formerly engaged in this industry have been killed or scattered. It is probable, therefore, that it will be some years before prices' will be materially lower. It would on this account seem an opportune moment to encourage expansion in this industry in Canada.

5.	The peculiar character of the industry in that it affords opportunities for gain to both farmers and artisans and to labouring men, women and children (for the last three as well as for the first under very healthful conditions) would seem to make it an industry well worthy of every effort on the part of any Government, to foster and encourage.
6.	Another peculiar feature of the industry, that it might employ a considerable number of labourers of all kinds in small centres close together which would not complete but rather, help each other by their actual co-existence in a country, seems to me most insistent of consideration.
7.	The sources of profit from the crop are: seed, cattle feed, oil; fibre for textile or cord making purposes; tow for upholstering purposes ; coarse, broken straw for packing and cheap upholstering; chaff for cattle feed; ligneous residues for fertilizer, or, possibly, other purposes.
8.	The production of this crop would seem to be indicated over the vast clay belt in Northern Ontario and Northern Quebec along the line of the Transcontinental railway, where soil and climatic conditions are probably favourable, as well as in western Ontario and over certain parts of southern Quebec.
Since writing the above sentence I have visited northern Ontario and on the line of the Transcontinental at Ground Hog river (Fauquier) I saw a field of excellent flax sown in June and just about ready to pull on September 24.	1
After reviewing what I have seen, the information I have collected and my interviews with different men interested in this industry, I would like to make a few recommendations along two lines.
Recommendations as to lines of effort likely to help the industry at the present juncture:
(a)	The urging aipon producers of the importance of grading their product, and, if possible, the assisting of them along this line. To do this it might be possible to bring over two or three experts from Ireland or from among the Belgian refugees in England.
(b)	The preparation and circulation of a brief pamphlet setting forth the possibilities of the industry and indicating the methods most likely ^to insure, profitable production.
(c)	The undertaking of a series of meetings during the coming winter in those parts of Ontario where the industry is already established. Such meetings should have for object the impressing upon farmers and growers of the necessity for better methods of producing and better seed. An effort should be made also at such meetings to show that flax is not a crop extraordinarily exhaustive of soil fertility.
# That would seem to be rather in conflict with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for South Oxford this afternoon.
The report goes on to make certain recommendations in regard to permanent work. By permanent work is meant the work that should be undertaken by the Government with a view of helping the industry in the near future and of putting it on a stable basis in such parts of Canada as may be found suitable as to soil, water, and climatic
conditions. The recommendations are as follows:
(1)	The establishing of a subdivision for fibre research work as a part of the Experimental Farms Branch.
(2)	The exhaustive trying out of varieties of flax and methods of cultivation on our various experimental farms in Canada and in addition at, say, three or four points in the present flax growing districts of Ontario, and possibly at two or three points in Quebec, where flax is likely to be successful.
(3)	The establishment on the Experimental Farm at Ottawa of a small but complete plant for all the operations in connection with the production of fibre from flax. Building machinery and equipment would cost probaoly $3,000 or $3,500.
(4)	The securing of a practical man such as Robinson, now employed by Fraleigh as a foreman in charge of the work there.
(5)	The employment of a young man with an Agricultural college training and an inclination toward this industry to go into the thing and make a thorough study of the practical side of the business for two or three years by performing all the actual operations, say at Mr. Fraleigh's until he could act as an. expert in judging growing crops of flax for fibre, in harvesting, in retting, in scutching, in sorting and grading, in baling, in hackling and in judging fibre. This man,, when adjudged to have attained a sufficient degree of efficiency, should be placed at the head of the work with fibre, either as a chief officer, or as a sub-officer of the division of botany; probably the former.
(6)	The appointment of a temporary officer in the outside service, attached to the experimental farms, who would take charge of the work outlined under first heading, and who might later develop into a useful man for outside work in this connection.
(7)	The continuation and expansion of the breeding work and selection work with flax now being carried on at the Central Experimental Farm.
That report was received some months ago by the Minister of Agriculture. The minister has been giving his attention to this question, and as a result instructions have been given along this line: First, that a properly trained man be selected to take charge of investigational work at Ottawa in connection with fibre flax production. Difficulty has been found in getting the right man for this positim, because, as is pointed out in this report, not many young men in Canada are experts in the matter of flax production. The department believes that it is on the track of such a man now, and it is hoped that '^n appointment will be made within a short time. Once we get a man who understands the flax business, the rest will follow as a matter of course. In the second place, instructions were given that a series of experiments be carried on in the different provinces, and that a special building be erected in Ottawa tnis season for the work in connection witn flax The

department is considering the question of bringing an experienced letter and scutcher from Ireland,' where the flax industry has assumed a very great degree of perfection. Special investigational work, with a view to approving varieties and methods will be undertaken at Ottawa and at other points where there are experimental farms. It is hoped that a series of meetings can soon be arranged for in the flax areas of Ontario, with a view to encouraging more of our farmers to grow flax for fibre this year.
These are the steps that have been taken. It seems to me that the result of these recommendations depends upon the qualifications, energy and industry of the man selected to take charge of this work in con-, nection with the Experimental Farm and the Department of Agriculture. If the department is fortunate enough to secure a man of ability who will take the matter up with enthusiasm, everything else will follow as a matter of course. The matter will be thoroughly discussed, and after experiments have, been carried on for a short time, I think it will be demonstrated whether it is expedient for the farmers of Ontario and the other provinces to extend their flax acreage and proceed with the manufacture of fibre from flax. The House will see from what I have stated that the Department of Agriculture has not been idle in this matter; it has given it very serious consideration, and has almost I may say, forestalled the resolution which has been moved by the hon. member for East Middlesex.

The suggestion of the hon. minister with regard to a proposed change in the resolution is quite satisfactory. When the resolution was framed I had not in contemplation the giving of a bonus or financial aid. I realize that there is a distinction between encouragement without aid and aid without encouragement. The use of the word " encouragement" meets the purpose of the motion, and I have no objection to the amendment.
Motion, amended as proposed, agreed to.

CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDING '	BILL.
Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough) moved the second reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
He said: I desire to make some progress with this Bill to amend the Canada Shipping Act which has stood on the Order Paper now for a long time. It is intended to give some relief to the toilers of the sea. The coasting trade of the Maritime Provinces is what I have chiefly in my mind, though, of course, the Bill affects the Pacific as well as the Atlantic coast.

The present law limits a coasting captain to 5 degrees north latitude; that is to say, he is not permitted to clear his vessel for any point further south than 5 degrees north latitude. The distance that the ship is al-_ lowed to go is governed by the kind of certificate that the captain holds. Under the shipping law of Canada there are two classes of certificates. One is called the deep sea certificate, and a man holding the deep sea certificate is at liberty to clear for any port in the world; there is no limit whatever, providing he complies with the law in other respects. A captain holding the coasting certificate however, is, as I have said, restricted at the present time to 5 degrees north latitude, sailing south.-My purpose is to change this, and to allow a captain holding a coasting certificate to go a much greater distance south.
Originally the law relating to coasting captains did not contain the restriction complained of. In the early days in the province of Nova Scotia, and the other Maritime Provinces, coasting captains were permitted to go as far as the owners of the vessels wished them to go, and they frequently took advantage of this liberty to sail as far south as Cape Horn, and even round the Horn. In the days of the gold mining in California, it was a usual thing for a coasting captain to go to California, and some of the more adventurous spirits went as far north as Alaska, to engage in the seal fishing. This continued for half a century or more. Those were the days when shipping flourished in the Maritime Provinces. It used to be the proud boast of Nova Scotians in the sixties-, that there was no country in the world that owned as many tons of shipping to the population as the province of Nova Scotia, not even Great Britain or the United States. That was in the sixties and the seventies, but I am sorry to say that that condition does not exist to-day, and I have no doubt that that fact is partly owing to the restrictions that have been imposed since confederation.
The ships of the Maritime Provinces were sent to all parts of the world in those days, and I have no doubt that the intercourse which the -people had with foreign countries had a good deal to do with the moulding of the Bluenose character as it is known today. The talk around the fireside on the winter evenings was about Shanghai, Nagasaki, Calcutta, Cape Colony, Valparaiso, San Francisco and other places far distant. It had the effect of making the Bluenose a sort of a roamer, for he is a wanderer, and has
been for generations. I think it was Sam Slick who said that wherever . you go throughout the world you can find a Scotsman and a Newcastle grindstone. I think it is also true that nearly everywhere you go you can find a Nova Scotian, for they are scattered pretty much all over the world. In those early days nearly every family had a son or a relative engaged in the deep sea trade, and of course they kept the people at home in touch with the great world outside. The ambition of the ordinary Nova Scotia boy was to grow up to be a sea captain. Among the published works of Joseph Howe there is a poem which is now out of print, and which contains a very interesting description of the coaster. I do not think it will be out of place for me to embalm it in the pages of Hansard. I know that the Deputy Speaker will not object, as I am quite sure a large number of his constituents are interested in the coasting trade in such places as Parrs-boro, Westport, arid other ports along the coast of the county of Cumberland, men who like those from other parts of that province, have distinguished themselves as hardy and adventurous seamen. The following is Howe's description of the coaster:
Though the idle may heed not, the wealthy despise
The race to which I and my fellows belong;
My voice o'er my own native waters shall rise,
And the deck of my shallop resound to my song.
Though my craft may be small, she is snug and she's trim,
And her crew are accustomed to battle the wave,
They are cheerful of heart, and athletic of limb,
And follow the business their bold fathers gave.	.
Through the storm and the sleet of the winter we sail,
While the rich and the feeble on couches repose;
There is health in our toil, and a charm in the gale.
And our courage still rises the harder it blows.	[DOT]
Every harbour from Sable to Canso's a home,
Every depth from the Banks to St. Lawrence we've tried,
And we care not though round Labrador we may roam,
Or sweep on the strength of old Pundy's fierce tide.
Now wealth from the wave we draw forth with our lines,
And now with a cargo of produce we're stow'd.
Or having a full freight of coal from the mines,
We slowly sail on with our cumbersome load.-

Though the Merchantman looks gay, her crew are hut slaves	.
And own not a stick of the vessel they steer.
Though the Frigate glides by, like the Queen of the Waves,
We know that the cat and the bilboes are there.
Then who would exchange the rough life that we lead,
Joint owners at sea, and free sons of the soil,
At the bidding of others to labour and bleed,
With hut little of pleasure to sweeten our toil?
We build our own shallops, we rear our own crew,
And life has for us sweet endearment in store.
For though luxury's fetters our souls never knew,
Bright eyes bid us welcome when peril is o'er.
Thus we Coasters enrich the fair land that we love,
And if danger should threaten, the cutlass we'd seize,	[DOT]
And our hearts and o ur sinews in battle would prove,
That the spirit of freedom is nursed by the breeze.	.

They would make good
men 'for a navy would they not?

I have no doubt that,
if the Minister of Naval Affairs would send out a call for naval recruits, he would find the young men along the coast of Nova Scotia just what Howe described them to be 50 years ago.
I refer to these historical matters for the purpose of showing what an important place the coaster has in the life and history of the Maritime Provinces. As I have said, the tonnage owned in Nova Scotia was much greater in the days of Howe than it is at the present time; that is a -regrettable fact. There was a ten per cent tariff and free navigation laws and the coaster to go wherever he could find business. The distance that the smaller class of vessel went was restricted by the size of the ship, because it is not profitable for a small vessel to go on a very long voyage as she cannot carry enough freight to make the venture profitable. Those restrictive laws which limit the distance unnecessarily are only hampering trade and doing good to no one. A vessel that can go 1,000 miles can go 2,000 miles, if she can find profitable business. That freedom prevailed up till Confederation, and after Confederation, but I think it was in the time of Captain Spain or Captain Salmon of doubtful memory that the officers of the Marine Department began
fMr. Sinclair.]
tinkering with the shipping law. They passed a regulation, which was ratified by Parliament, that a captain holding a coasting license could not go further south than Cape Hatteras. That shut out the coaster from the West Indies, where his most profitable trade is to be found in the winter season.
Many of our ships that are engaged in the fishing industry during the summer season, when winter comes and fishing on the banks is closed, were accustomed to find profitable trade with the West Indies. They frequently carried down a cargo of lumber or fish and returned with molasses or rum. That was the course of trade for many years. Then this unfortunate restriction was imposed by which they were not allowed to go beyond Cape Hatteras. This shut our vessels out from trade with the West Indies. This continued for several years, until the statute was repealed in 1908 and the line moved down to 5 north latitude, which enabled our coasters to engage in the West Indian trade. But that is not far enough. Our larger ships can find more profitable business in South America. Since the war began, the larger class of coasters in the United States have done a very profitable business along the coast of Brazil and the Argentine Republic. This business has chiefly been done by the vessels of the United States. Their laws are so free from restrictions that a captain of a coasting vessel up to 700 tons needs no certificate at all. The owner of the vessel selects his captain, puts him aboard, and the Customs House asks no questions. That is the law of the United States, and you can readily see what an advantage it gives ;their seamen over ours, who are .subject to these restrictions in competing with the United States for that profitable trade. Shipowners naturally tried to discover some method of evading this regulation. The coasting captain is a resourceful fellow, and he did discover methods of evading the law. One method was by securing the services of a deep-sea captain to clear his vessel. In many ports of the Maritime Provinces can be found some old retired sea-captain who has served his time at sea and holds a deep-sea license. The Customs House cannot refuse to clear a ship when a man holding such a license is in charge. The consequence was that the owner of a ship would temporarily employ one of these retired men for the temporary purpose of clearing the ship. The deep-sea

captain would get his clearance from the customs house for some port further south than the law would allow a coasting captain to"go. The old captain would then sail his ship down the harbour, and at some convenient headland would go ashore and the real captain come aboard and go on with the voyage. The law was evaded in that way for several years, but it was found very inconvenient, for these old captains were not always on tap, and I have heard of one case where the captain thus temporarily put in charge refused to give up the ship after he had cleared from port. So they had to find some other method, and the next one adopted was to change the registry of the ship. That has been frequently resorted to. The result to-day is that about sixty or more of the largest coasting vessels in the Maritime Provinces are registered in Barbados; a few are registered in Newfoundland or some other colony.
There is no difficulty about changing the registry of a ship; it is just as easy as rolling off a log. The Government provides the necessary machinery, and that is what makes the whole proceeding look so extremely foolish. All that an owner has to do when he wants to evade this regulation is to go into one of the offices of the Canadian customs and ask for a blank form, which is provided freely by the Government. He then fills it out, signs his name, and his ship is transferred to Barbados or wherever elese he wants it registered. He pays the trifling sum of three or four dollars to the customs officer, walks out of the office, pulls down the Canadian flag, and goes on with his business. That is what has been going on for many years, until now a great number of the vessels that were under Canadian registry have been transferred to the -registry of some other colony, or to that of the United States. And a great many more ships would have been transferred to United States registry during the past two years if it had not been for the Order in Council which prevents ships from being transferred to any foreign registry during the war. Everybody knows that until about two years ago the American registry was closed to foreign vessels. If a citizen of the United States wanted to own a ship he had to build it in the country. Then, in the early summer of 1914, a law was passed in the United States allowing an American citizen to purchase a ship and place her under the American registry without paying any duty, and subject to
no special restriction. Between that date and the outbreak of war no less than fourteen vessels had been transferred from Canadian registry to United States registry, and had it not been for the Order in Council passed by this Government many more Canadian vessels would have been transferred to the American flag. As I have already said, some of our vessels are even now under the American flag, and many others are registered in some distant colony. The reason why they register in other colonies is because the ships of these colonies are under British law and are not subject to the restrictions that exist in Canada. A vessel registered in Barbados, for example, is permitted to sail to South America, and to carry on business where business is profitable. This is the definition of a coasting voyage as it stood in the revised statutes prior to 1908:
Coasting voyage means a voyage between any port or place on the Eastern coast of Canada and any other port or place on such coast or in Newfoundland, Labrador, St. Pierre, or Miquelon, or on the Eastern coast of United States, not farther south than Cape Hatteras; and on the West coast not farther south than the harbour of Portland, in the State of Oregon.
That was repealed in 1908 and the line moved down from Cape Hatteras to 5 north latitude. I propose now to repeal the present section and to substitute therefor the following:
" Coasting voyage " means a voyage between any port or place on the eastern coast of Canada, and any other port or place on such coast, or in Newfoundland, Labrador, or St. Pierre or Miquelon, or any port or place on the eastern coast of the United States of America or Mexico or Central America or in the West Indies, or on the eastern coast of South America not further south than forty degrees south latitude; and also means a voyage between any port or place on the western coast of Canada, and any other part or place on such coast, or on the western coast of the territory of Alaska, or of the United States of America or of the western coast of Mexico or Central America or South America not further south than forty degrees south latitude.
If this Bill becomes law the Canadian coaster will be permitted to compete for business in the ports of South America. I see no reason why he should not go round the Horn. The American coaster is at present free to engage in South American business. What I *am asking for is that a captain holding a coasting License be allowed to trade with South America, and go through the Panama canal, and be free to do business in the ports of the Pacific coast.

Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me that capital is very sensitive, especially capital engaged in shipping. The man who owns a ship is in a much more independent position than the man who owns a railway, or a telegraph line, or any similar enterprise on land. It is the easiest thing in the world for a shipowner to seek new fields, and if need be to change the registry of his ship. If the Canadian trade is not profitable, he can leave Canada, and engage in trade in Europe, in the Argentine Republic, in the West Indies, in India, wherever there is profitable business. He has the seven seas to go to, and, consequently, when this Parliament imposes upon him a foolish restriction which hampers his business, he simply pulls up his stakes and goes where laws are reasonable and business is profitable. That shows how important it is for Parliament to be careful in regard to such restrictions. In the United States, for example, not more than a year or so ago, some labour organizations raised an agitation that Japanese and Chinese should not be employed in vesels plying out of the ports on the Pacific coast of the United States. Congress capitulated to this agitation and the consequence was that they passed a law prohibiting foreigners from being employed as sailors on American ships. At that time California was the headquarters of a large shipping firm which had a fleet of ships trading in the Pacific and calling at Honolulu, and proceeding to far eastern ports. This firm was compelled to retire from that business and use their vessels elsewhere, because they could not comply with the law. They could not get American sailors to man their ships, and now the only communication which the people of the United States have with far eastern ports is by Japanese vessels, and there is now no regular liner flying the American flag sailing out of any of the Pacific coast ports of the United States. That is humiliating to the United States, and has happened because of that simple regulation that I have referred to in regard to the employment of sailors, so that restrictions of this nature which may appear simple enough to landsmen and people who do not understand shipping matters, frequently turn out to be very serious when applied to shipping interests where capital is sensitive and where it is open for a shipowner to escape from the scope of such regulations.
Now, there are still a good many coast-

ing vessels on the Canadian register, and we want to keep them there; but if we are to do so, we must act promptly in order to prevent more of them from leaving. Two years ago I introduced a Bill intended to rectify this difficulty by repealing this clause and allowing the coasting captains to sail further south. At that time the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who I am sorry is not in his seat, postponed any action in the matter, stating that he intended to revise the shipping laws of Canada, and that then this matter would receive his attention. So far as I know nothing has been done, and the consequence is that since that date two things have happened: a large additional number of ships have withdrawn from the Canadian register, and those which have remained under the Canadian flag have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars for their owners, who are penalized by the loss of profitable business which they cannot engage im because they are not allowed to sail to southern ports. The question is often asked, why is such a regulation as this in our Statutes? I confess that I am not able to answer the question, and I do not believe my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is able to explain it. The question has been asked over and over again in this House, and no one has ever been able to answer it. The restriction apparently was made owing to the whim of some one in the office of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and it is difficult to understand why it has been allowed to remain in the Canada Shipping Act for so many years, seeing that it has done so much damage to the shipping business of this country. If it was a question of safety, I would not complain. If safety was the object one would have supposed that restrictions would have been imposed upon captains sailing to northern latitudes in the winter season; but there is no restriction so far as going north is concerned, the only restriction is against going south amid the laughing waves and eternal sunshine of the topics. The Minister of Customs never hesitates to allow a captain to clear his ship in the dead if winter for the stormy shores of .Newfoundland, for Labrador, for Baffin bay, for that new country where Stefannson planted the Canadian flag last year. You can go as far north as the North Pole if you wish; the Minister of Marine and Fisheries offers no objection to a northern voyage, but as soon as you turn the prow of your ship south, he says, "No, you must not go there,

because it is past 5 degrees north latitude," but he gives no other or better reason, and no man in this House or outside of it has ever been able to give any better reason why that should be the case. The restriction, however, has stood on the statute books of Canada for a good many years, and it reflects on the intelligence of the Canadian parliament that it should remain there.
The size of the coasting vessel does not justify the restriction because some of these vessels are large enough to sail anywhere; they can go across the ocean just as easily as along the coast; they are quite capable of sailing any sea and weathering any storm. They do not usually cross the ocean because it is more profitable for them not to do so. Many of them are too small for long voyages. At the same time the average of these ships is larger than the ship in which Columbus crossed the ocean on his eventful voyage. If my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had been in power in the days of Ferdinand and Isabella, Columbus would never have been allowed to sail outside the straits of Gibraltar; he certainly would not have been allowed to cross the Atlantic. If I remember rightly, the Pinta was only 90 feet long and 25 feet wide, whereas many of these coasting vessels are of much larger dimensions and tonnage.
