The Chairman of the Railway Commission, Sir Henry Drayton, had been taking up with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane), a. few days prior to Mr. Cochrane's departure from Ottawa, the question of trying to relieve the situation in the West in so far as the movement of grain is concerned. When I took charge of the department, I found a ldtter from Sir Henry Drayton to the minister. In this letter Sir Henry Drayton explains the situation in connection with the movement of grain in the West, and suggests the passage of a Bill similar to that which I have placed before the House. I believe the best way to explain this Bill to the committee is to read the letter which was sent by Sir Henry to the Minister of Railways. It is so complete, and, I believe, so interesting, that I think it should be placed on record. It reads:
Ottawa, February ISth, 1916.
Re Grain Crop.
Dear Mr. Cochrane;
The Railways have been faced with an exceedingly difficult problem in the transportation of the very large grain crop of the North West.
I make no complaint whatever as to the manner in which the railways have moved the crop during the past season. On the other hand, the movement was extremely good, surpassing all records. It is sufficient to say that from September 1st, 1915, to January 15th, 1916, the railways had transported no less than 53,920 cars of grain more than were hauled in marketing the large crop of 1913, and extending over the whole period required to market it.
I fully realize the importance of the service to the public and the fact that the result could not have been obtained had not the railways been efficient and properly operated. While this is all true, however, the present condition is unsatisfactory and calls for some special remedy.
The Department of Trade and Commerce places the crop (all grains) in the Western Provinces at 723,664,000 bushels, as against 322,056,000 bushels for 1914, and 503,267,000 bushels for 1913. At a low estimate, 300,000000 bushels remain to be carried; and unfortunately a comparatively large percentage of this total, as to which only an approximation can be made, is without proper protection.
The tremendous crop of this year is such that the elevator capacity of the country cannot commence to contain the balance of the crop, even in view of the fact that no less than 191,323 cars have already been transported up to the 15th of January last.
Temporary granaries have at different points been erected, hut over and above the grain in elevators and in temporary granaries, there is a large amount of grain which has been left out all winter, either in stook or already threshed and covered with straw. This grain, while subject to danger of some deterioration, will largely be saved, provided it is moved before the spring rains set in.
The grain on the Grand Trunk Pacific has been largely marketed; and the Board has now no serious complaint of congestion on its lines. This, of itself, does not show any more efficient management on that system, as the crop tributary to this line is much smaller than the volume tributary to the Canadian Pacific and Canadian Northern Railways.
The Grand Trunk Pacific has moved approximately 15 per cent of the present crop, and they will be in a position in the near future to handle grain to a considerable extent that may be offered for transport.
The Grain Commission reports congestion on the following Canadian Pacific Railway Lines: Outlook Branch, north of Moose Jaw; -Empress Branch; Vanguard Branch; South of Lethbridge. There is also complaint as to congestion on the Weyburn-Shaunavon Branch.
The' Grand Trunk Pacific has moved approxi-tion on the Canadian Northern Railway on the following lines: In the Goose Lake District; Moose Jaw-Gravelburg Branch; Saskatoon to Regina. And also state that outside of Manitoba every Canadian Northern point has grain which should be moved.
Again, in so far as delays in the movement which have occurred since the close of navigation are concerned, no complaint is made as against the railways. These delays were largely inevitable. Firstly, owing to the fact that, generally speaking, there was but comparatively little available storage in the East; secondly, that, owing to the war and the commandeering of boats, the supply of bottoms was limited; thirdly, because of the embargoes obtaining largely, and frequently absolutely, at all grain shipping sea ports; and fourthly, congestion of traffic, which was even more marked in the large American terminals than in our own winter ports. In addition to all this, weather conditions and the necessities of the coal movement would, in any event, have prevented any free or general movement of grain traffic.
The situation, however, as I see it, demands

that the ordinary traffic conditions must be departed from, in order to save a large portion of the crop, and the ordinary rules of traffic should be at least temporarily disregarded. The railways should co-operate closely with each other and move the crop as soon as possible, irrespective of the fact that traffic returns of the originating road may be diminished.
The crop on the Canadian Northern Lines has been very large. Notwithstanding the fact that that Company carried a large percentage of the grain already transported, perhaps 35 per cent, an estimate made by the Company of grain still to be marketed on its lines in the prairies amounted to 53,232,480 bushels, and in elevators adjacent to its system 36,000,000 bushels, making a total of S9,232,480 bushels to be hauled.
The Company has since reported that the total grain still in the farmers' hands and unmarketed amounts, according to its estimate on the 15th instant, to 32,844,000 bushe'.s of wheat, and 15,402,000 bushels of other grain; so that the total grain still in the farmers' hands is reduced from 53,232,480 bushels to 48,246,000 bushels. The result is that the Canadian Northern has on or tributary to its system in the Prairie Provinces 84,246,000 bushels of last year's crop yet to be transported.
The congestion which the Grain Commission complain of as the worst in the country is on the Saskatoon-Drumheller, and De Lisle-Elrose lines, running through what is known as the Goose Lake District.
I should also say that a deputation from this district waited upon the Honourable Dr. Reid, when acting as Minister, and was referred by him to me, with the request that I would see that everything possible should be done to relieve the conditions there obtaining.
The Company advises that in this district and adjacent to its lines, there are 11,732,000 bushels of wheat and 1,945,000 bushels of other grain yet to be marketed, or a total of 13,677,000 bushels.
I take the situation here as illustrating the need of relief, again making no complaint against the Canadian Northern, but merely to illustrate the demands of the district and the necessities of the farmers, which are the more serious, in view of the fact that, generally speaking, there was a crop failure in this district last year.
These thirteen million odd bushe-s represent wheat which has not yet been carried to the elevator, much of which will be subject to damage, unless the grain is moved, as already stated, before the spring rains.
The figures as to grain storage in the district show 7,063,900 bushels, making a total of 20,740,900 bushels of grain to be handled in this district alone.
The matter has, of course, been carefully canvased by the Board with the Company, and the best service Mr. Spencer, the Board's Chief Operating Officer, was able to get the Company to say would or could be given to the district was 150 cars a day. In view of the conditions of operation on the line and the failure of the water supply, which has resulted to a large degree at least from excessive winter conditions, it is extremely doubtful whether the Company could possibly move this number of loads; but, assuming that the Company could load them and should commence this movement
on the 1st of March next, which is probably the best that could be hoped for, owing to the fact that the line has only recently been opened after the winter storms, and that water conditions are still bad, it would take, if the movement was maintained, until the 15th of next July to market the crop ; or, on the other hand, if the amount of grain in storage is deducted from the calculation and only the 13,677,000 bushels yet on the farmers' hands considered, the amount could only be moved by June 1st. This, of course, would be altogether too late to save unprotected grain.
The usual rule is that a company should be entitled to the traffic of its own lines, and to the business of that part of the country which it has opened up by its enterprise and the expenditure of its capital. This rule may be said to be of general application, applying, not only in Canada but also in the United States and in Great Britain. It is fair; but only fair, as it occurs to me, when the company can handle that traffic within a reasonable time. This rule gives the Canadian Northern the benefit of the long haul from the Goose Lake District to the Lake Elevators.
I am very free to admit that it would be foolish to expect the railways to move the whole crop in any given year before the close of navigation; and that, if it was so moved, it would probably be the worst thing that could happen for the farmers themselves, destroying to a large extent the value of their product by the consequent depression of the market price. On the other hand, any condition of transportation which results in the western farmer being unable to market his crop until the following June or July, is just as unreasonaoie.
The condition of the farmers in the Goose Lake district for example, to-day is that in so far as the 13,677,000 bushels of grain already referred to are concerned, they cannot market it, and owing to lack of storage facilities, for which of course the railway is not at all to blame, they will be unable to save a large percentage of it under the present transportation conditions.
It should be possible to increase the movement on this line by proper co-operation between the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Companies. The Railway Act does not enable the board to order this to be done; and I recommend that the Act be amended on the lines of the amendment now enclosed.
It is extremely doubtful that if the traffic moves under ordinary conditions the Canadian Northern will be able to look after more than 100 cars a day. It would appear, however, that if the maximum number of cars and engines were supplied and placed in service on the branch, and instead of being run through to eastern points, made delivery in the Saskatoon elevator, where weights and inspection can be obtained, and were then taken on by the Grand Trunk Pacific, the movement could be very greatly accelerated.
The grain should move at the present through rates, without additional expense to the farmer. The ordinary rate per mile which the rate from Saskatoon would make should be reduced and the through rate should be apportioned so that a greater mileage return should be given to the Canadian Northern, in order to make its-shorter movement profitable. As the resultant business to the Grand Trunk Pacific would be largely found business, as it has idle engines and equipment, some reduction in the regular

rate would be fair to that company. Apart, however, from any railway concerned, but treating the matter merely in the public interest this action or some similar action is necessary.
It well may be that, as the movement develops, similar joint traffic arrangements will be found necessary at other points, both on the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern lines.
It is but fair to say that what I propose is an extension, and perhaps a radical one, of the joint traffic requirements companies are now subject to, owing to the fact that a single line route, reasonable and direct, has been already provided, and also that the movement, although * by joint operation and subject to the additional handling charges entailed thereby, will nevertheless move at the ordinary rate in so far as the shipper is concerned. The fact that the single direct route is congested and unable to move the traffic, coupled with the exigencies of the situation, affords, however, as it occurs to me, an ample justification for the proposed action.
As to the urgency of the situation, there does not seem to be much room for argument; and, if in your view, that situation can be remedied on the lines proposed, might I suggest that the Bill be immediately introduced and its passage facilitated?
Yours faithfully,
H. L. Drayton.
The Honourable
The Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Ont.

I have not discussed that
point with Sir Henry Drayton. I understood from Sir Henry Drayton that, whatever the rate was from any point on the Drumheller section or any other point on the Canadian Northern railway from a point east of Drumheller on to Fort William, the farmer would pay the same rate even if the grain went through this elevator and right through to Fort William. I suppose that this Bill
was suggested by the Chairman of the Railway Commission.
Yes, he wrote the Bill.
The word "board" undoubtedly means the Board of Railway Commissioners; it means their interpretation of the clauses of the Railway Act. This Bill enlarges the powers of the board.
Yes.

It enlarges the powers
of the board to deal with special cases in which where one railway company is not able to handle the congested traffic, other railways can be asked to assist in the relief *of that congestion; and the board is given the power to distribute the rates among the different railways.
Mr. REID Yes.

It may be asked whether this could not have been done without an Act of Parliament, but I do not think it *could, for the reason that the regular railway tariff as to mileage and hauls will be disturbed by this arrangement; that is to say, the rate on the short haul usually allowed will not be allowed under this arrangement, and the rate on the long haul may be changed to comply with the special conditions. Undoubtedly, the railway companies themselves could not get together and make a joint rate under those conditions, because the proposed arrangement disturbs their haul arrangement. This gives the board a power which it did not possess before, to step in and arrange the rates under these peculiar conditions. Neither the Chairman of the Railway Commission, nor any member of the board could do it without this Act.
That is it exactly.

I think that the letter to the Minister of Railways from the chairman of the board, who has studied the case closely, makes it desirable that we should facilitate this Bill so that it may go through the House and to the Upper Chamber and become law as soon as possible, because every day lost in the movement of the grain makes it much more serious for the farmer.

- I have not blade any particular inquiry into that, but I have inquired as to the duties performed by the present officials and compared them with those performed during the past four or five years, and while the revenue has decreased somewhat I do not know that any great reduction could he effected by any reduction of the officers. mise I am sure I shall be only too pleased to listen to suggestions.

He is not strong for
economy.
And not tax him too heavily after he gets there.

We have tried to make taxes as reasonable as possible. First of all, we try to give the miner security of title. When my hon. friend from Edmonton was Minister of the Interior, he put through this House a Bill which incorporated the regulations of that day into the Yukon Placer Mining Act, and from that time to the present every one in the Yukon has
been satisfied as to the question of title to property. Millions of dollars have been invested in the mining industry in the Yukon because of the law passed by the hon. member for Edmonton when he was Minister of the Interior. When a miner goes out into the wilderness we want him to feel that the Government is behind him, so far as title is concerned. These men then go out Into the hills and valleys, and sometimes find it difficult to get more than what they call their grubstake. 'In some cases the Government, feeling that it is in the interests not only of the Yukon but of Canada as a whole, has paid the way of these prospectors. If a group wanted to go to an outlying district, the Yukon Government would appropriate a few dollars to carry these men to that distant point. Then as regards mail service, we have had to subsidize some boats running on the tributaries to the Yukon, and it must be remembered that some of these tributaries are navigable for from 250 to 300 miles from their juetion with the Yukon. The territory up there is vast, but I am sorry to say the population is sparse. We have not the population we had years ago, but it is a vigorous, a hardy and adventurous population, a population specifically and peculiarly fitted for a great territory like that. I venture to say that there is not an army in Europe to-day, and that Napoleon never led an army, that was better, physically and morally, than the army that crossed the White Pass and developed the gold' mines of the Klondike in 1896. Many of those men and many of their children are still there. They have erected schools, and for the information of the House I might say that in the public school of Dawson we give the first year's course in the University of Toronto. We do not call it a High school or a Normal school, but the students can matriculate from it to McGill and Varsity. We could not do that without money; we could not do it unless the Federal treasury was behind us. The suggestion was made the other night that the Yukon should unite with British Columbia and I did not have an opportunity then to express my disapproval. The part that is developed is in the same

proportion to the whole territory as a postage stamp is to a post card, and we have huge areas that have never been trod under the foot of the white man. Why should we wish to be tacked on to British Columbia, particularly as we receive assistance from the Federal Government?

That is in the abstract, but I submit that there is no specific case.
Perhaps not, but my information is that there has been such a case.

I accept my hon.
friend's statement, but I do not think there was a case of that kind. But, even so, it was only an interim appointment; Judge Macaulay was only out of the territory for five or six months and at the expiration of that dime he returned and took his place on the bench, while Air. Black, who had been acting as interim judge, stepped down and resumed his duties.
He did not give up his duties in the lower court while performing his duties in the higher court?
In what capacity?
As administrator.
That is not a court.
Yes it is.
No, it was never so considered in the Yukon. I am sure that at one time the public administrator was not a lawyer at all.

To what court could any person who wanted to appeal from the public administrator apply for redress unless to the court over which the public administrator presided?
Mr.'THOMPSON: I have no doubt that the procedure indicated by the hon. gentleman would be quite correct, and that an appeal would lie from the public administrator to the judge of the Territorial court.
While the public administrator was acting as judge of the court any appeal from his conduct as public administrator would necessarily have to be taken to himself as judge of the court.

I admit that if there were appeals that would probably be the procedure, but I have never heard of a case being taken from the public administrator in the Yukon {o the judge of the Territorial court. However, if there were such a case what would be the result? The man who . had, this fantastic grievance, if he had a grievance, would simply have to wait until Judge Macaulay returned. While we all understand the procedure in the court, what would my hon. friend think of this? He speaks of an appeal from a judge to the same judge. Judge Macaulay for years had been acting in the Yukon Territory as Police Court Magistrate, again meeting the argument advanced by the hon. member



for South Renfrew, and this was done while he was- a minister of the Crown and for the purpose of effecting economy. While Mr. Macaulay was sitting as Supreme Court judge he was also acting as Police Magistrate. The culprit was apprehended by the Northwest Mounted Police, brought before Judge Macaulay, sitting as Police Magistrate, he had his preliminary trial before Judge Macaulay as Police Magistrate, he was committed for trial by Judge Macaulay as Police Magistrate, and then was tried by Judge Macaulay as judge of the Supreme Court.

Does not my hon. friend see -the distinction between that and the case of a man who is handling the estate of widows and orphans, and from whose conduct as public administrator during that period, no appeal could be taken except to himself?- It must also be remembered that the public administrator is in receipt of fees and commissions. From what this party told me it seems to be quite reprehensible that the Government should appoint a gentleman occupying a position of responsibility and trust in connection with estates to a position which would take away any right of appeal from his conduct as public administrator except to himself as judge of the court.

The distinction is so great that I cannot imagine the two things from the same standpoint at all. In one case it is a imatter of dollars and cents; in the other case it is a matter of life or death, and very frequently, a matter of personal liberty. In the one case, 'the man who came before the public administrator, only had to wait until the judge, in fact, returned which at the most, was a matter of six months. In the other case, there was no possibility of the man getting out of it. He was arrested by the police, committed by Mr. Macaulay as police magistrate and tried by Judge Macaulay as judge of the Supreme Court. The only appeal he had was to Judge Macaulay of the Supreme Court. How can you measure these two cases by the same standard? In that instance the Government did it, and I tfynk they were right in doing it from the standpoint of economy. But, here is the milk in the cocoanut. You could meet my hon. friend's criticism by creating another official. But by not doing so, looking at it from the standpoint of economy, you save a little money, but I 
question whether it is good economy or not. Mr. Black to-day is acting in the capacity of judge of the Territorial court. Judge Macaulay has gone on a vacation. He had a murder case to try at Whitehorse, 400 miles from Dawson, just before the close of navigation. He came up to try that case, and, if my memory serves me right, navigation closed while he.was there and he could not get back without going by the same line. While he was at Whitehorse he wired to his chief, the Minister of Justice, for permission to come out for a further vacation of three months. My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that the lawyers in the Yukon have their vacation In the winter time, when there is very little to do, instead of in the summer time when they are quite busy. Judge Macaulay wired for another furlough, and the Minister of Justice very kindly granted this to him. He is spending his winter at Belleville, Toronto and Montreal. Again, we had to have some one to act as interim judge, and we choose the man who acted with so .much satisfaction before. I have never heard of any criticism in the whole of the Yukon Territory of the conduct of Mr. Black acting in his capacity as interim judge. Even his political opponents admitted that he made a good judge. My hon. friend knows him very well. He knows that he is a gentleman of long experience at the Bar and <5T considerable attainments. When Mr. Black acted before-the same applies to his present service-he did not receive one dollar by way of pay, although he adjudicated upon several intricate and important cases in the Yukon.
Then he was clerk of the court, public administrator, and judge?

He not only was, but is now. He is considerable of a Pooh-Bah, but he is a good Pooh-Bah. I am anxious that my hon. friend should not overlook anything; I may mention that he is also legal adviser to the Yukon Council.

What does he get for
that?

What does he get as
clerk of the court?

I really do not know positively; about $7,000 a year, I think, altogether. The records show: salaries of the

Territorial Court sheriff, and clerk, $4,000 each,
Is he sheriff, also?

No. We are great
economists, but we do not think it wise to add the office of sheriff tp his other duties.

Is he sheriff, and
then announcer, and then judge of preliminary inquiry, and then judge of the session, and then hangman; does he perform all these functions?

He is not sheriff, oi
hangman, or jailer. There are many things that he is not.
He is so many things that we have to find out what he is not.
If the hon. gentleman had been more assiduous in his attendance upon this committee, he would have heard just what this gentleman is and just what he is not.

I may tell the hon. gentleman that when the Yukon Territory was organized two judges were named, Mr. Dugas and Mr. Craig. The Supreme Court of Canada is, I understand, the Court of Appeal for the Yukon.

No, the Court of
Appeal is the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

When Mr. Congdon was
the Crown Prosecutor I had to defend the Yukon murderers, Labelle and Fournier, before the Supreme Court of Canada as the Court of Appeal of the Yukon Territory Am I right or wrong?
Right.

Since that time, has any
change been made?

Yes. I told the
committee before my hon. friend came in, that at one time appeal lay from the Yukon court to the Supreme Court of Canada When the court en banc was abolished, appeal was taken to the Supreme Courc o( British Columbia, and that is where we have our appeal now. If litigants wish to cary their cases further, I suppose they can carry them to ,the Supreme Court of Canada. We have only one judge there now.

I thought you had two
judges.

We had three judges, but we retired two. Mr. Black is interim judge while Judge Macaulay is on his vacation. Primarily his position is clerk of the court; he is also legal adviser to the Yukon Council and public administrator.
How much does he get for his services as public administrator?

He is paid in fees;
he gets five per cent of the estate.

To what court does the administrator apply for letters of administration, and to what court are his accounts submitted for examination and approval1 Would it not be to the very court which he was appointed to preside over in Judge Macaulay's absence?

I do not deny that.
There is but one court in the Yukon, and if there were an appeal, it would have to go to that court.
That would be to himself, during the time that he was acting as judge. Does my hon. friend remember a case in which the judge, as police magistrate, tried a case in which he himself was a party?

No, he never did anything of that kind. I defy any one to name a single case in which he sat in both capacities. I know my hon. friend wants to be fair, but he is wrongly informed. I say here on my responsibility as a member of the House that Mr. Black would not do that. My hon. friend would not do it, I would not do it.
That is not the question; it is a question of jurisdiction, that is all.
There is no question of jurisdiction, the jurisdiction is clear. He is acting in the three capacities at the present time.
What capacities?
Clerk of the territorial court, interim judge, and public administrator.
I am sorry for these three offices.

My hon. friend may be wasting his sorrow. I have not heard any sorrow expressed in the Yukon where he administers these estates and deals with these cases. The people there are satisfied; I have not heard a complaint'. It is they

whose judgment should 'be taken in this matter. I . admit that in normal times, with big revenues and a large population, this condition would not be permitted to exist; but the basic reason for this course is economy, which has been so strongly urged upon the Government by hon. gentlemen opposite.

There is one thing I cannot understand. As a clerk, he would act for himself as a judge; and, being a judge, he would act for himself as a cleTk. Then, being a clerk and a judge, he would act for himself as a clerk and as a judge as a court of appeal. We had something of the same kind in Montreal when Judge Sieotte was clerk of the peace and was acting as magistrate of the court of en-quete and sitting as clerk of the court of King's bench on the criminal side. We objected very strongly to that. If you want to economize there are many other things in which it is possible to economize in the Yukon. The things which are important to the citizens are, first his life, then his liberty, and then his property. This man being a judge, and a clerk, and a sheriff, in the morning at 9 o'clock he, would sit as a clerk, at 10 as a judge, and at 11 as sheriff-or hangman. That is what I object to.

My hon. friend seemed to think I was criticising the conduct of Mr. Black. I used to know Mr. Black in New Brunswick, and I should be very sorry to say anything as to his conduct since he has been in the Yukon. I have no reason to suppose that it has not been exemplary. What I complain of is the action of the Government in appointing a man to all these different positions. It would appear to me that Mr. Black was receiving a very large income indeed. He is
10 p.m.' public administrator of the whole Yukon territory, and my hon. friend says he gets five per cent of all the estates which he administers as public administrator. This must bring him in a very large income indeed. Then he is clerk of the court, from which office he gets, my hon. friend says, $4,000 a year. He is advisor of the Yukon Council, from which my hon. friend says he gets $500 a year; and there was something else, what was it?
Hangman.
I should suppose that in all probability Mr. Black's income would reach the very large sum of $15,000 or $20,000 a year.
Oh, no.

Do not let my hon. friend make any mistake. There have been many wealthy people in the Yukon, and, despite the invigorating climate of that country, some of them must die, as in other parts of the world. My objection is to this man being the administrator of estates and also being the judge of the court before which these estates may be brought in litigation. Thus ^people are deprived of the right to bring the administration of these various estates before -the court for proper judicial review. No Government should take a course that would deprive people of that right. The positions of clerk of the court and judge of the court are entirely inconsistent, and it is particularly absurd to say that one man in the Yukon, Mr. John Black, who, when in New Brunswick, was a most ardent Conservative, as I suppose he is still, should be made a perfect Pooh Bah and occupy all of these positions, to which considerable emoluments are attached. It is 'not only unjustifiable, but I say it is disgraceful that the Government should appoint one man to all these various positions.
Would this not be a good time for the minister to let us know what of these Estimates are to be actually expended and what are not? The Minister of Finance informed us that there were some $29,000,000 in these Estimates which the Government did not ifttend to expend during the coming year. The Minister of Finance pledged the good faith of the Government to this statement. We have been considering Estimates for a number of days, off and on, and so far we have had no statement from any minister as to what of the Estimates in his particular department are to be expended and what are not. The time has come, in my humble judgment, when this committee ought to be informed upon this point. We ought to know from the Minister of the Interior which of these amounts which he is asking for are to be expended. We have a right to assume that, before the Minister of Finance made the statement he did, the question had been considered in Council. It was a most important statement to make to the people of this country and to their representatives in Parliament. A very large amount is involved. I want it understood that the members of this House on both sides who do not ' occupy the treasury benches have a right to be ihformed upon this important question. I think it is only fair and reasonable that we should ask the Minister of the Interior to give us informa-

tion upon this point before we go on to consider these items. Surely the Minister of the Interior will be able to give to the committee that information as far as his department is concerned. I would ask my hon. friends on both sides of the House if we are asking for anything unreasonable when we make this demand. We are here representing the people, and are supposed to take, as we are desirous of taking, an intelligent view of these estimates, in order to judge whether or not we should vote the items. We have a right to know which of them are to be expended, and which are simply here upon paper and are not intended to be acted upon. Why does the Government bring these Estimates before us at all, unless they want our judgment upon them? We are not here simply to record, the views of the Government; we are not here simply to hear the Deputy Speaker read out these items, and then to pass them without some intelligent idea as to whether or not they are required for the public services during the coming year.
I appeal in the best spirit to my hon. friend the minister to inform the committee as to which of these items it is intended to expend and which it is not deemed necessary to expend for carrying on the public services in his department.
Perhaps I might be permitted to add a word.
Let the minister answer. My hon. friend might divert his attention.
My hon. friend is not going to divert my attention.
I have asked the minister to reply.

If the minister
wishes-
Perhaps he does wish; I have a right to ask him to reply.
I do not know why the hon. member for St. John is putting up this sham fight.
It is no sham fight, as perhaps you will realize before we *are through.

I have not refused to give any information that has been asked. I allowed the hon. member for the Yukon to reply to the question because, as my hon. friend realizes, he is much more conversant with the matters of that Territory than any other member of this House, and he can answer as to the local conditions
better than I can. We are now on the item relating to the Government of the Yukon Territory. If my hon. friend had been present the other night he would have heard discussed many of the things we are . talking' of now. Are we going over these items and rehash them every time a member comes into the House, and waste the time of the House giving members information time and time again. If the hon. member for St. John wants an answer about these particular items, I may point out that they are divided into three:
Salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the Territory; grant to Local Council, and grant to Local Council for main-tenace of and repairs to roads.
The first is the item we have been discussing; the two others are fixed items which are requisitioned by the local council. The expenditure is under their jurisdiction; we do not expend this money. We vote it to the council, and they expend it. They have spent more than we voted. Take the expenditure on roads. The item for last year was $100,000; they have expended $140,000. Then in salaries and expenses, the vote was $128,000 and out of that amount we expended $115,000. It is not possible at all times to have right down to a dollar the exact amount which we are going to spend. I do not think that the margin between $128,000 and $115,000 is very large.
I have not refused to give any information, and I do not think I deserve a lecture which I have received from the hon. member for St. John.

The minister has been
very fair, so far as those particular items are concerned. He speaks of my putting up a sham fight; what would he think would be a real fight? I am simply doing the best I can, as a member of this committee, to get information, and I would expect support from my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). When he was a member of the late Opposition he was very watchful; he was a perfect watchdog, and I would expect to have his co-operation. I am glad to see him here to-night, glad to see that he has come back. I appeal to my hon. friend from Peel to say whether I am not right. We must treat the Government as a whole. The Minister of Finance has informed Parliament and the country that although there are printed h$re in black and white numberless items, including the Estimates of my hon. friend, amounting altogether to the enormous sum of $189,000,000, it is the opinion of the Government that it will not be

necessary to expend $29,000,000 of that amount. I ask the Minister of the Interior in all sincerity if he thinks it is right to keep the members of this committee in the dark as to what the items are which, in the opinion of the Government, it will not be necessary to spend. I ask the minister whether he will not be good enough to tell us what items there are in his department, the expenditure of which will not be required. Then we will be able to help him along materially. I have seen the Opposition in this House do a great deal to facilitate the passing of Estimates, but we want to be treated fairly. I am not asking for anything but fair treatment when I ask this information to be given to the committee.

Perhaps I may now be permitted to refer to the discussion which preceded the remarks of my hon. friend, and to. point out to the hon. member for St. John that in combining the offices to which he referred, the Government have followed the policy carried out by the late Government with great success, the object simply being to economize. The only estates of which Mr. Black acts as a public administrator, are estates in connection with which no will has been made, and, they are not large estates.
Cases of intestacy.

Yes. There are
not very many of them, and they are very small. I would not undertake to say how many hundreds of dollars a year he gets, but it does not amount to anything like the sum my hon. friend mentioned. Furthermore, when he sits as judge, he does not act as clerk of the court; the sheriff acts as clerk of the court. But this whole matter can be easily arranged if my hon. friend wants it. It would be an easy matter to get a clerk of the court and a public administrator.
It is about time the judge acted as his own clerk.
He does not act as judge and clerk of the court at the same time.
He is the real clerk.

I am not denying that. It is all a question of economy. We can get other men to do the work, if that is what is wanted, but we have been trying to meet the exigencies of the territory.
f Hr. Pugsley.l
I think you could get two or three men to do the work at no greater cost than is involved in paying this one gentleman this enormous salary.
Is there any official stenographer in the Yukon?
Yes, George Craig and Harold Blackman; their salaries will be found in the Justice Estimates.

When I suggested that
some of the offices in the Yukon might be amalgamated, I had not in mind the offices that have been described by the hon. gentleman to-night. The minister got a bit cross with me for asking for some information with regard to the cost of the government of the Yukon Territory, but I think the information that has been given out tonight makes it clear that I did not make any mistake in asking my question. The minister himself says that he is asking for $13,000 more than he expects to spend.
That was last year.

Well, surely my hon.
friend is not going to spend more this year than last. Could he not cut this $13,000 out? That would take a little off the $29,000,000 that the Government does not expect to spend. The minister says that he has made a reduction from last year, but that does not affect the statement of the Minister of Finance that approximately $29,000,000 will have to be cut off these Estimates. We on this side of the House are doing all we can to back up the Minister of Finance in getting this reduction made, and I think the minister might make a start. The country should know just what the Government intends to spend. It is not fair to the country as a whole, nor to the taxpayer, to allow this $29,000,000 to stay in the Estimates, and it will militate against the borrowing power of the Government,	because	when the
Government goes to the markets of the world, they will have to explain why they have expended $29,000,000 more than they should have expended, according to the Minister of Finance. It is not fair to the country, and it is not fair to the House for ministers not to intimate what items they do not intend to expend, nor is it meeting the wishes of the Finance Minister, who says that there are now in the Estimates $29,000,000 more than ministers should be allowed to expend.

I do not think the Minister of Finance had reference to the Interior when he stated that there were amounts in the Estimates which it was not intended to expend. When the Estimates were being made up, I gave instructions to have them prepared with a view to the strictest economy, and some that were submitted to me I sent back with the request that they be reduced if it could possibly be done without impairing the public service, and I received memoranda back from those in charge of the preparing of the Estimates to the effect that they had been prepared on the lines indicated, and they did not see how the Estimates could be reduced without impairing the public service. That, in short, is the position of the Department of the Interior. There have been certain reductions this year, but as regards the ensuing year I do not think there is any large amount at all in the Estimates that we could say for a certainty will not be expended.

Does the minister say that the Finance Minister made his statement to the House without the matter having first been brought before the council and carefully considered? Was council not informed how the $29,000,000 was made up?

I think the hon. member knows pretty well that when the Finance Minister made that statement, his attention was directed principally to those Estimates in the Public Works Department, which were re-votes, and in regard to which work would not be gone on with this year.
That accounts for only about $5,000,000.	,
How many judges are there in the Yukon territory?
One judge.
I see by page 32 that the judge gets a travelling allowance of $500, and a living allowance of $5,000. Then, as sheriff he gets $4,000, and $4,000 as clerk, which makes $13,500 altogether.

The judge is not the clerk of the court. This item would be clearer if it were written out as follows: Salaries of the Territorial court officials, such as sheriff-, clerk, etc. The judge does not get those salaries.

Perhaps the minister would explain how this $128,000 was exr pended last year.
It is found in detail on page K-162, vol. 1, of the Auditor General's Report.
I see the Hon. George Black gets a salary, of $6,000, and a living allowance of $6,000. What relation is he to Mr. John Black?
A nephew.
They have done pretty well.

That could surely be left out in this time of war.
Seeing that we are at present engaged in the work, we should not have any break in it. We have our staff and we might as well keep them at work.
If they are all young men, perhaps they might want to enlist.

They are not all young
men.

From the statement of the minister, here i-s an expenditure of

$260,000 which is not required during the coming year. It is not required half as much as the expenditure on public buildings, but it is proposed to keep men at
work in investigations and demarcations of the exterior boundaries of Canada. Does this mean the provincial boundaries? How ridiculous it is that we should be now defining the boundaries of two provinces; although, I assume that as these are exterior boundaries, they must be the boundaries between Canada -and the United States.
That is what they are.
Is there any necessity for that?

It is being done jointly
with the United States.

That is very true, but
the United States would not complain if, by reason of the conditions due to the war, this work was allowed to stand over. The minister should bear in mind that the Minister of Finance has felt himself obliged to come down with proposals for taxation which mean the imposition of very heavy burdens upon all the business interests of this country. The minister must be aware that, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, complaints are coming in to the Government, as they are coming to the private members of this House, that the proposed taxation is going to be very burdensome. Not only is the minister proposing to put taxation in the future upon the business interests of this country, but he is proposing to adopt a principle which has not been recognized as a correct one; he is proposing to pass retroactive legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must respectfully
ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the subject under discussion. I cannot see any connection between retroactive legislation and an item of $291,000 for scientific institutions for the Department of the Interior. I hope my hon. friend will try to confine his remarks to the item .under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I am
sure that you would not be unduly narrow in your rulings in regard to this question.
I do not want to question your ruling, but I see the error of it and the difficulties into which we would be led if it should prevail. It would mean that I could not point out the reasons why the Government at this time should - not ask for this large vote of $260,000. What reason can I advance?

Is not the financial position of the country the very strongest reasons which a member of this committee could urge against the voting of this large sum of money? Is not the fact that the Minister of Finance comes down and tells us that he cannot get along without imposing heavy burdens upon the business interests of the country, and not only imposing them for the future but taking them out of the pockets of those who have been carrying on these industries in the past year and a half, and thereby imposing retroactive legislation?' Surely, Mr. Chairman, you do not mean that I cannot give the reasons-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member that-his remarks might be very proper in the Committee of Ways and Means, but this is the Committee of Supply and the rule is very clear that the discussion must be confined to the item under consideration.

Then, I move that this item be struck out, and I will proceed to give my reasons, which I think will convince the committee that it ought to be struck out. You, Mr. Chairman, speak of the difference between the Committee of Supply and, the Committee of Ways and Means. How can you vote Supply until you know that you will have the means to pay the money you vote? How can the Government ask . the committee to vote $260,000 unless they are going to state to the House the means by which they will raise that money? The two committees of Ways and Means and of Supply are indissolubly connected. Before the Government come and ask this House to vote any sum of money it ought to be in a position to say what it wants the money for. How is it proposed to raise this money to pay this $260,000, which is a part of the $189,000,000 which it is proposed to raise? The Minister of Finance, when he lays his Estimates, amounting to $189,000,000, on the Table, said: " we want a vast sum of money and how are we going to raise it? I am going to ask this House to raise it by imposing taxes upon the business interests of this country among other things; we are going to raise it out of customs, excise, and from other sources, but by reason of the vast amount of money which- we want for the ordinary services of the country we intend to impose this taxation upon the business interests of the country." I could not present to this committee any stronger argument in favour of
striking this item out than by mentioning this fact. Where is the necessity for it? I could understand that if there was an abounding revenue we might indulge in- this unnecessary expenditure; we might go on with our investigations and demarcations of the exterior boundaries of Canada; we might even take up triangulation, levelling, topographical work, geodetic surveys and astronomical work. We might do all that if we had the money to spend, but when there is distress all over this country, when people are contributing of their means for patriotic work and when (he Minister of Finance comes down and demands that this extra burden of taxation shall be imposed upon the people, it is not a time to expend a vast amount of money which is not necessary. I appeal to every member of this House, as to whether I am not right in that. You may say that this is only $260,000, but, after all, this forms a part of the vast sum which the Government are calling upon Parliament to vote. The Government have not the money to warrant them in expending this sum and in order to obtain this money, which is a part of the vast millions which they are demanding from the people, they are proposing to impose the extra taxation.

Where is Canada after all? Do we not know yet? Notwithstanding the Treaty of Paris of 1763, we do not know the boundaries of our own country. We require a triangulation, an investigation and a demarcation to ascertain the pxterior boundaries of Canada. It. seems to me that we are quite behind the time. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Thompson) was talking about the Alaskan boundary a few moments ago and now we have to spend $260,000 to find out the boundaries of our own home. I am perfectly sincere in what I am going to say. If this item refers to the salaries of the men who are employed in this work, I am willing to vote for the payment of salaries because I do not want to deprive anj man of his salary. He is accustomed to receiving his salary; he has based his system of living upon it. But why should we spend a large sum of money to find out whether Mount Stephen is 5,000 feet or 3,800 feet above the level of the sea? We know what lake Superior is;, we know what the prairies are; we know what the Rockies are; why should we spend a large sum in finding out whether Mount Washington is a few feet less than a certain

number of feet above the level of the sea? When we are spending a million and a half every day on the war, why should we spend a quarter of a million dollars to find out whether the ice at Glacier is colder than,the ice at lake Louise? I read a few of the items:
Investigations and demarcations of the interior boundaries of Canada.
We are living in peace with our neighbours in the United States; could we not postpone this expenditure while the war lasts?
Geodetic Survey of Canada.
I suppose we shall have to find out how many cubic feet of water flow daily over Niagara Falls; possibly $25,000 would cover that. We shall have to find out also whether the level of the sea has increased or decreased.
Astronomical work. Department of the Interior.
It will be necessary to ascertain, I suppose, when Venus or Mars will meet the bun. I agree that those employed by the department should be paid their salaries, but no other expenditure should be made.
What portion of the International Boundary Survey is included in this item?

The Ontario-Minnesota
boundary, and the boundary between Quebec and New Brunswick, and the adjacent states.

Surely there cannot be much of this international boundary incomplete; the work has been going on for many years. So far as this vote is required by reason of an agreement with the United States, it is my view that it would be unwise not to provide the money necessary to carry out that agreement. Would the minister say whether the work proposed to be done is called for by agreement with the United States,?

Yes, by article 5 of the treaty of 1908. The commissioner in charge of the matter in the United States is providing a vote to carry on their portion of the work, upon the understanding that we carry on ours.

We are friendly with the United States; is there no way by which we could communicate witlji President Wilson or members of the United States Government, with a view to post-

poning this expenditure of $260,000? One cannot walk on the streets of Ottawa, Quebec or Montreal without being appealed to in some form or other, for funds for war purposes. I am giving as much as I can, and you are giving just as much as you can. Are we going to' spend $260,000 to secure the delimitation of the boundary between this country and the United States? By all means let us live up to our obligations under the treaty mentioned. But I suggest that hon. gentlemen opposite would be rendering a great service to their country if they could save a quarter of a million dollars by suspending this expenditure for the present. I would feel disposed to give it to the Minister of Militia for the purpose of serving the Empire and our country.
This $260,000 is not all appropriated for the delimitation of the boundary between the United States and Canada. Only $25,000 is for that purpose.
Save that.
Save the rest; save it all.

If the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John were adopted, the result would be just the condition of affairs that the hon. member for Laval would deplore. $40,000 of this vote is for salaries of officials, who would be deprived , of this amount if the vote were eliminated. Parties are prepared to go out in the spring on this work; 'their salaries also would be sacrificed. I think it would be very ill-tjudged action on our part if we were to adopt the motion of the hon, member for St. John. As the hon. ex-Minister of the Interior justly states, we are carrying out our agreement with the United States in finishing this Ontario-Minnesota boundary line. I believe there are about 120 miles yet to be marked out.

The minister says it
will cost $25,000.
For the Ontario-Minnesota boundary.

How is ,the $235,000 to
be expended?

I read all of that a few
moments ago. The Ontario-Minnesota boundary, $25,000; the Quebec-New Brunswick and adjacent states boundary,. $25,000; boundaries generally, drafting, printing,

etc., $10,000; geodetic survey, astronomical work, general expenses, etc.-
How much is the geodetic survey?
What is that survey?

It is somewhat scientific,
and I think that the work done under this vote is not less for the Interior Department than fob some other departments, including the Public Works and Militia Departments.
I was Minister of Public Works, and I never was able to see where it was of the slightest advantage to that depar^meno. I never utilized it and never could see how it could be of any advantage.

I am informed by the
officer in charge that it is for the purpose of accurately determining points which will serve as bases for surveys of all kinds. The triangulation is to be continued. The precise levels are being determined in various parts of the Dominion. The total mileage of levelling to-day is 9,000 miles.
How does the vote for this year and last year compare with those of the past four or five years? Has it been increasing or decreasing during a period of say five or six years?

There was a considerable
decrease, I understand, last year, and the vote is exactly the same this year.

It seems to me the minister has struck the crux of the question when he says that it would necessitate the disbanding of some of our parties and that men would be thrown out of employment if this vote were reduced. Why should they not be thrown out of employment at a time when individuals and communities are saving every dollar they can to carry on the war? Why then should the Government spend money on things that are absolutely useless? We know how these things are done. They have a number of officials and the minister says: We must keep these men employed. They have a lot of men employed oil these surveys, and it simply serves to keep them going during the summer. Why should not these men devote their time to something else, go to work and 11 p.m. really earn some money? Many of these men are ordinary labourers, or young men going through college, and in order to keep up the supply of
money for these people, this enormous sum is being paid. This Government does not realize for a moment that the country is at war and that immense sacrifices are being made. As long as they can borrow money by millions, they say the country is prosperous, and that they will keep this army of officials in employment. It has been pointed out that there are 11,000 or 12,000 more people in the employment of the Government to-day than there were four or five years ago. In order to keep these
11.000	useless employees of the country going along at high salaries, the Government says: if we do not vote this money we cannot keep our people going. The minister says it is necesary to spend $25,000 this year in order to delimit the boundary between New Brunswick and Quebec, and the neighbouring states. So far as the New Brunswick-Maine boundary is concerned, that was settled in 1842. The lines were then run out and, many years ago, this Government, in conjunction with the United States Government, surveyed it, and they have had party after party going over the country the last five years making re-surveys. The part of the boundary which is on land is marked by concrete posts which are in sight of each other, and on the lower and upper parts of the line, where the boundary is the 'St. 'Croix and St. John rivers, the boundary posts are set up on the shore in such a way that at any turn in the river engineers can determine from these posts, within six inches, the exact location of the line in the middle of the river. I am thoroughly familiar with the situation there and to spend money to delimit that boundary at this day is simply throwing away that amount of money.

This $25,000 would keep
25.000	soldiers for a day.

If the rest of the work, between Minnesota and Ontario, is of the same character, and I suppose it is, as that between New Brunswick and Maine, the money there is simply being thrown away too. The geodetic survey might be of some use to scientific men in later years, but what use can it be to the people of Canada to-day? As I understand, it is a scientific process by which certain base marks are provided, and engineers or surveyors can go by them and by testing out can see whether their instruments are absolutely accurate and whether the levels of the water are correct to the tenth of an inch. That may be interesting from a

scientific standpoint, but of what use is it to the people of Canada to-day when every man, every woman, and every child are iepriving themselves of the real necessities of life in order to raise money to carry on the war? If there is a vote which has been - proposed by the Government during this session that ought to be struck out-I was going to say root and branch, but perhaps a few dollars should be retained to carry out treaty obligations-this is the vote. The minister, 1 hope, will take this into consideration, and if he cannot stop all of this expenditure, let him at least stop most of it and try to save $200,000 of this useless waste of money for surveys that have been completed and that age only kept up in order to provide salaries for a lot of political friends of the Administration.

I am very anxious to see that the obligations of the country are carried out, especially in regard to the boundary, but I must say that I was very strongly under the impression, like the hon. member for Carleton, that the boundary survey, as required under the treaty arrangements with the United States, had been completed some time ago. If it was not it seems to me that that would be a point on which to make the criticism that there has been undue delay in the administration of my hon. friend, because, when I left office, I am sure the work had progressed so far towards completion that, at the same rate, it should have been completed before now. If this proposed survey is merely something in addition, something that is not absolutely called for by our treaty arrangements with the United States,
I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Carleton has said.

Since there has been so much objection on t'he part of hon. gentlemen opposite, I am willing to let the item stand for further consideration. My information is that the particular item referred to, the survey of the boundary line between the United. States and those provinces is the result of the treaty, and it has not been completed. It is work that has been progressing since before this Government came into power, and it did not receive any opposition when my hon. friends were in office.
Things were different then.
Yes, there was another government in power.
There was no war.
And the work was not finished then.
I thought it only right that .we should continue the work and complete it, but if hon. members desire this item to stand I shall offer no objection.

While the geodetic survey may be an entirely desirable means of information when we have the money to spare, it is a fact that at the present, time money is required not only for war purposes, but also for the development of necessary enterprises in which this country is now very heavily engaged. I am bound to agree that under these circumstances the work of the geodetic survey might be suspended for a period.

Before this matter is
disposed of, I would like to ca'l the attention of the minister to the fact that from his statement there would be at the very most $50,000 in regard to which there would1 be any possibility of an implied obligation to the United States to complete the survey. That reduces by $210,000 the amount which it seems to me it is necessary to expend at the present time.
What about the $40,000 for the head office?

I do not understand that any gentlemen are engaged in this work at the head office but those who have permanent employment. Take Dr. King; he is a very eminent scientist, but he is employed at the head office at other work. He is the chief of the Astronomical Observatory, and so with others. Tnere is a good deal in what my hon. friend from Carleton said that in connection witn this work young men, students of the universities, are employed temporarily. Every young man to-day who is able and willing to work can get employment of various kinds. Then we know there are a great many men in the service who are enlisting, and the men who are permanently on the staff might very well be engaged to replace those who have enlisted instead of bringing in new men. I think the minister should reduce this vote by $210,000 at least, and on the understanding that he will give us a statement as to how he proposes to expend this money I shall withdraw my motion and let the item stand. The minister must not think for a single moment that we are raising these objections

from any narrow standpoint. We have a duty to perform, and that duty is to point out, if we can, to the minister that, in respect to various items which come up for consideration in the Estimates, the expenditure is not required in the public interest, particularly at this time when the war is on, and in view of the enormous taxation which it is . proposed to impose on the ->
people. We are trying to discharge our duty; we hope to do it firmly, and with some degree of intelligence, but we must do it persistently, and we must not allow these items to go through as a matter of course.
T should just like to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works who is leading the v House that the work of the Government would be greatly facilitated if they would make up a list of the items comprising the $29,000,000 or $30,000,000 contained in these Estimates, which the Minister of Finance guaranteed to Parliament and to the country will not he expended because they are not required for the public services. To-night we are to a large extent in the dark. We do not want to obstruct the estimates of any minister; we want to facilitate their passage, but we also want to have the consciousness that we have done our duty,^ and, so faT as we can, prevented the passing of unnecessary Estimates. If this information were given to us, it would greatly facilitate our work, and, I am sure, the work of the Government. With that understanding, I will withdraw my motion and the item can stand.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
